utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are following these procedures. Welcome back again after the summer break. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Tolimir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I would like to call for appearances because it's a very special day or a special week. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Peter McCloskey and Janet Stewart for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the Defence. I see Mr. Tolimir is present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to everybody present. I wish that we have a successful continuation of all this and that everything is completed according to the God's will. Present on behalf of the Defence are myself and Mr. Aleksandar Gajic. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is our first sitting since 21st of February of this year. We are sitting today for the closing arguments in this case. The Prosecution and the accused filed their final trial briefs on the 11th of June, 2012. I would like to go to private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Both final briefs of the parties were translated on an expedited basis by Friday, the 20th of July, as requested by the Chamber. I should like to thank the translation unit, the CLSS, for the special efforts it has made to ensure that the translations were completed before the summer recess. I recall that the Prosecution will be presenting its closing arguments today and the Defence will be presenting its closing arguments tomorrow, and that on Thursday each party has an opportunity to present a rebuttal of 30 minutes' duration if it wishes. This morning there was informal communication from the Chamber to the parties about 15 exhibits which are at the moment marked for identification. I would invite the parties to be prepared to deal with that matter to resolve the final administrative problems on Thursday after the end of the closing arguments. Mr. McCloskey, before I invite you to make your submissions, I should remind you that they need to be completed by the end of today. Please bear that in mind. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I first want to tell the Trial Chamber that it has been an honour to be in front of you and I thank you for your courtesy and your professionalism. As much as it can be in a case like this, I can tell you it's been a pleasure to be before this Tribunal, before this Court. It's been a long trial, but you've allowed us, both the Prosecution and the Defence, to put on our cases. We've not been rushed. And that is more appreciated than you can imagine. I want to thank the Defence team of Mr. Gajic who did a very good job and came on when they were very much needed, the staff of this courtroom, especially the interpreters, and my team, Nelson Thayer who is not here with us, Kweku Vanderpuye, Rupert Elderkin, Abeer Hasan, and of course Janet Stewart. Now the plan today is for me to speak to you for about a third of the time, concentrating on the significant contributions of General Tolimir to the joint criminal enterprise to murder, what we refer to as the murder operation. After me Kweku Vanderpuye will take roughly one-third and discuss the same thing regarding General Tolimir and his responsibility of the forcible transfer charges. The last third will be divided by Rupert Elderkin and Abeer Hasan. Mr. Elderkin will speak to you of the opportunistic killings and murders that occurred and Ms. Hasan will speak to you of the impact of the victims and how that relates to the genocide. So I will try not to overly repeat what we have said in the trial brief. I do want to address some of the defences that were brought up, but this is finally a chance for me to put the key factors and evidence in one targeted approach, hopefully within an hour, an hour and a half, and so I will be going over some of the most important contributions of General Tolimir. From 13 July through 16 July and even beyond that, the VRS summarily executed over 7.000 men and boys of Srebrenica. This horrendous crime was ordered by Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic and carried out by elements of the Main Staff, forces of the Drina Corps, and the forces of several Drina Corps brigades. All of these forces you are by now familiar with and I won't repeat them here. The murder operation, the JCE to murder the Srebrenica men and boys, was organised and overseen and implemented by the intelligence and security administration of the Main Staff led personally by General Tolimir; organised, overseen, and implemented on the ground by his chief of security, Colonel Beara. Beara was assisted on the ground by the chief of intel Colonel Salapura and Main Staff intel officer Colonel Jankovic. The Main Staff security worked closely with and professionally supervised the Drina Corps security branch, in particular Colonel Vujadin Popovic, together with the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade security units, Captain Momir Nikolic, Bratunac; Lieutenant Drago Nikolic and Milorad Trbic of Zvornik. The murder operation was carried out and implemented with exceptional discipline, organisation, and efficiency. In no less than four days the VRS murdered an enormous part of the Srebrenica population of men and boys. And this was largely due to the experience, efficiency, and cold ruthlessness of the security branch and their work with the commanders in carrying this out. General Tolimir must bear responsibility, as he led this murderous group. The operation was conducted in a traditional military command according to the principles of the VRS and the chain of command was strictly adhered to. Without the military organisations working together, as they had throughout the war, with well-trained discipline and a solid chain of command, there is no way the VRS could have murdered over 7.000 Muslim men and boys in just four days. The adherence of the chain of command and military discipline is what allowed this terrible crime to be committed so quickly and efficiently. The fact that the VRS remained disciplined, organised, and respected procedures in the chain of command is an essential foundation by which all the evidence must be reviewed. It does not by itself of course negate the Prosecution's duty to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the contributions of General Tolimir. But once we see this working as it should with the people in the places doing their job, it provides you with a very important foundation by which to judge all the evidence. The Defence is of course very aware that a functioning chain of command is a -- undercuts any defence they have and is something they must attack, and they do. They first do it by quoting Mr. Butler, who very succinctly stated the position. On July 8th Mr. Butler stated in part: "The fact that a military has been ordered to carry out an unlawful order doesn't mean they're going to carry it out in a non-military manner. A military organisation is just that, it's an organisation. It operates along a defined structure and hierarchy." He goes on to say: "Despite the involvement in unlawful acts, the people that a commander needs to involve are those military professionals who by training and by profession are responsible for making certain activities happen within a military organisation." Mr. Butler went on to explain General Tolimir's and the Main Staff responsibilities and their job and tied that into the crimes as our brief and has been the focus of most of this case. The Defence challenges Mr. Butler and says that that did not happen. In their brief they say that for a mass murder to be conducted by the VRS, there must have been some deviation in the customary practices in the chain of command. Now, they say that but then they don't provide us with any deviation; and frankly, we don't see any deviation. The evidence doesn't reflect a deviation. That's why we spent so much time with the procedures, the rules, the documents, so you could see that this thing was functioning as it should. The only deviation that we see is that instead of caring for the prisoners in their custody as they should and delivering them safely and securely to the Batkovic prison camp, they delivered them to the killing fields of Orahovac and Petkovci and other places where they were in a systematic and organised fashion summarily executed by firing squad. The only thing the Defence really tells us is that General Tolimir was in Zepa at the time. Now, of course there's nothing -- this is no deviation. Perhaps we're to infer from the fact that he was in Zepa that he was somehow not involved, but of course as you know Zepa is within the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, it's very close, very connected to the Srebrenica events. General Tolimir was within comms the entire time that he was there, and as chief or as the head man of the intel and security of the Main Staff, he was clearly responsible for the events that are going on in the Main Staff as well as his responsibility in Zepa. So by purely saying that he is in Zepa provides no defence whatsoever. And to suggest that he is not involved in the Srebrenica events is a flat-out misstatement by the Defence. Of course we'll go over and see soon, he is constantly writing and making proposals regarding the Srebrenica events and the prisoners that he's learning all about there. Perhaps there is another defence which we haven't heard frankly, that Mladic sidelined Tolimir for some reason. We have no reason why. We all know Tolimir is a brilliant strategist, a hard worker, he knows his job better than anybody else. And remember the witness said lo to the man that keeps information from General Tolimir. The Srebrenica murder operation was one of the most important and critical aspects of this war. Should that secret have gotten out, it could have changed and did change the history of this war. Mladic needed his top man on this. Why on earth would Tolimir have been sidelined? Though they don't say that. I would think it. I would suggest you would think it. There is no reason. They give us no reason. Perhaps there is a suggestion that it is because he is an honourable man, a man of faith, that would not be involved in the mass murders, and therefore he was set aside from this. This is not said anywhere that I can see. But there's one document in this case that destroys that Defence, and it's not ever my position to come into this court and judge people personally. That's not what this is about. It's about criminal responsibility. But there's one document in this case that is the most insidious document I have seen in my career here or that is in this case, and it's drafted by General Tolimir and it shows the depth and the deprivation that he was willing to go during this war. This is Exhibit P488 and it's one of the few exhibits that I want you to take a look at, if we could. You'll remember this is dated 21 July 1995. It is in the middle of the attack on Zepa, a few days before the Zepa population is forced out. The Zepa troops are holding out, they're in that amazing terrain that you saw, in caves, in ravines, they're very hard to get at by the VRS. And from his position near the Rogatica Brigade Tolimir sends out this proposal to -- personally to General Miletic, the chief of operations and the person that's clearly involved and able to communicate with Mladic and others. You can look briefly at the first three paragraphs. It just provides intel, information, and others. And then Tolimir goes on to say: "We believe that it would be more favourable to hold direct negotiations after inflicting losses on the enemy's military personnel. We request the means for crashing the enemy's defence in the sectors of Brezova, Ravna, and Purtici." Negotiations from a point of military strength is normal, it's fine. But then this is what he says: "The best way to destroy them would be by using chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs. Using these we would ... the fall of Zepa and the surrender of the Muslims." Now, a lot has been made of these chemical weapons. We know -- as we all know this is tear gas, and the tear gas in a combat can be used to ferret these people out of these places and then shoot them down. It's not something that you could tell with the VRS officers we talked to wanted to talk about. But that's not really what I'm talking about here. That's not what concerns me so much. Yes, he wants to use these weapons to ferret people out and he wants to use what are fuel air explosives which detonate in the air and can bring people out of these areas, if you recall Mr. Butler's testimony. And he's suggesting this is the best way to take down the army. And then this is the part that I'm getting to. "We believe that we could force the Muslims to surrender sooner if we destroyed groups of Muslim refugees fleeing from the direction of Stublic, Radava, and Brloska Planina." Here he is simply proposing that refugees, civilians, be destroyed in order to get the army to surrender sooner. This is a calculated and vicious and criminal proposal. As you could see from the reaction of the various VRS officers we asked about it. It's not a question of translation. I asked General Obradovic read it and tell us what he said about it, and he said, Oh, this means attacking civilians and that's not what the VRS was about. And then he opined for the first time that was a misinformation. It could be part a misinformation campaign by General Tolimir to scare the enemy. And that fell apart because as you know this is a proposal for chemical weapons, and we saw the chemical weapons come personally to General Krstic through very confidential means. So this is a real document. General Tolimir did not adopt this idea that this is a misinformation. It was a real document. There's nothing in his brief that this is misinformation. This is General Tolimir doing what he feels needs to be done to win the object: Get the Muslims defeated and get the population out the of Zepa. He is willing to do Mladic's bidding, he's willing to do what it takes. One of the reasons we're here is because in the 20th century targeting civilians in large scale was a common practice to bring countries to their knees. We're here to stop that. General Tolimir tried to make it happen. I don't know if it happened. We don't know if shells fell on civilians up there, but the fact that he is able to target civilians, women and children, provides a clear indication to you that he is capable of leading an operation to murder the able-bodied men of Srebrenica. There's no reason to bring Tolimir out of the chain of command. He is the man that will get the job done. He will do what it takes. Now, I'd like to get into the specifics of his involvement. In any human endeavour where people are organised to achieve a particular purpose, be it military, diplomatic, business, academic, legal, or whatever, there are periods of crisis, where planning and decision-making and directions become particularly important and intense; and it's during these times that communication is vital. It's also, as we see during these periods of crises or critical phases that the VRS was most likely to let their guard down and perhaps put something in a document that they wouldn't have otherwise or say something over an open line. And so what I've done is I've divided this case into ten critical phases roughly along chronology, but I don't want to be bound by a pure chronology, and talk to you about each one of them and General Tolimir's involvement in them. The first critical phase is around that period of 11 and 12 July when there is a potential for the VRS to capture large numbers of Muslim men and boys in Potocari and that on -- and on the 12th of July that same potential, to capture the fleeing Muslims that are going through the woods. Do we see General Tolimir getting involved in this critical phase right before the decision to murder the men from Potocari? Well, the first thing we'd look at is his job responsibility. Capturing prisoners in large quantities and interrogating them and dealing with them and getting them securely transported, does that -- is that something he fits? Well of course it is. That's why we spent so much time on the military police, the security job, the responsibility to oversee the military police. We see the documents from Popovic, from Beara, even Tolimir about the military police. Also did Tolimir get involved in large group? Of course he did. We see that from the evidence. Remember, we spent such a long time with Mr. Butler going over the history of General Tolimir and all the various prisoner exchanges he was involved in, from the little to the big, from the beginning of the war onward. So not only is it in his job description but up until July 11th, 1995, he had been doing just that for large numbers of potential prisoners and prisoners. So he should have been involved. Was he? Well, on the evening of 11 July that we know from Momir Nikolic, and from the reality of the situation, that a thousand able-bodied Muslim men could be viewed from VRS positions and this was reported up the intel chain. These were the men that were later separated in the next two days. Was Tolimir aware of this? Absolutely. How do we know that? We know that on the 12th of July, the very next day, he travelled by car to Bijeljina, where he met with Todorovic, the East Bosnia Corps security officer to arrange for 1.000 to 1200 prisoners reception at Batkovic. We know this from Todorovic, we know this from Tolimir's driver. So clearly Tolimir at this point is keyed in on these 1.000 potential folks even before they're separated and arrested. Also the day of the 12th we know that the army and the civilians are fleeing through the woods and this is when the VRS gets a good intel grasp that most of them are heading in the direction of Cerska and on towards Tuzla. Does General Tolimir become aware of those folks? Well, the answer is absolutely yes. We know that because he comes back from Bijeljina on the evening of the 12th and stops by Vlasenica, the Drina Corps headquarters, according to his driver. And we see two documents authored by Tolimir that come out of the headquarters, both of which deal with the subject of these fleeing groups. And he says, and I quote, in the first one which was Exhibit P02203: "Prevent armed Muslims from illegally reaching Tuzla and ordered to arrest them." Of course, we need to take prisoners. The next document he sends out shortly after that in the late evening is Exhibit D64, and it talks about the same topic and says: "To prevent the withdrawal of enemy soldiers:," and I quote, "and to capture them." So he is fully involved in knowing about the men in Potocari, the men in the woods. At this point who is captured and who is not has not really happened yet as far as he knows. And then Popovic sends a report to the Drina Corps saying that they've kept -- they're keeping separated men and Tolimir should have seen that. And in the same document I just mentioned, we can see that he is aware that men are being separated and kept because he says after talking about capturing men from a column: "Note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari." This means he knows the separations and is keeping these men. There would be no reason to note their names down if he is merely referring to men that are being shipped off to Kladanj. It serves no purpose to note their names. The men go off to Kladanj, they return to the BiH, the names don't mean anything to them. It's only if they're going to keep them and screen them, which, as is their right, to determine if they're good intel sources, if they're perhaps war criminals, they're perhaps army that they can keep to exchange. So he knows about that. He knows that those men are being separated and he sends out this order, to note down names. Now, the next -- I will comment on what that means in our view relating to his knowledge in the murder operation. And that brings the next critical area, and that is the decision to kill the approximately 1.000 Muslim men that are in Potocari. And there is no evidence in this case that General Tolimir was consulted before that decision was made or that he was involved in the original decision. In fact, the very fact that he suggests that he ordered lists be made is completely inconsistent with the murder operation because that would create the evidence of the crime, and we never saw lists being made of this murder operation except for a small time in Nova Kasaba when Mladic came and stopped that list being made, as you recall. But in Potocari, with Mladic present, with Popovic present, no lists were ever made. It would not have been made. So that's an indication that by the 12th of July Tolimir has not been engaged in that. He's been on the road to Bijeljina, he's been up in the East Bosnia Corps which has not been brought into this as yet. And the one thing we learn from expert Ratko Skrbic that wasn't complete nonsense was that in any operation it's essential to keep it as closely held as possible and it only goes out when it needs to go out for the operation to succeed. So Mladic and his people in Bratunac. And they hadn't even been able to arrest the people from Potocari yet. I don't believe they contacted Tolimir. So at that point we don't see Tolimir involved. But it is important for your deliberations to determine when the decision to murder the men at Potocari took place. And as you should recall, it's always been the Prosecution's position that this happened sometime the night, the late night of 11 July when Mladic and Krstic, Zivanovic, Popovic were together at the Hotel Fontana and they found out about these men and before the 10.00 meeting when Mladic announced that he would be screening the men captured in Potocari, men 16 to 70. So clearly by the morning meeting when Mladic says men 16 to 70 will be screened, Mladic has made a decision what to do with these men. What was that decision? Well, go to the testimony of Momir Nikolic, it's very clear. Popovic after the meeting tells him to begin separation processes and identify areas that these men will be killed. Nikolic gives him the name of the Ciglane, the brick factory, the Sase mine. Now, Momir Nikolic, any person that testifies pursuant to a plea agreement, a plea agreement that was involved in the events, must be viewed with great caution by you. You need to carefully look at everything he says and it is that material that's corroborated that can be used in your judgement. But in corroborating this kind of evidence you can look to the entire set of facts and circumstances. One thing to look at in this particular case, the Ciglane brick factory. Look to Deronjic's testimony. This is, according Deronjic, was where Beara was trying to kill people on the 14th. And it's no coincidence that Beara is using the brick factory and Momir Nikolic has told Popovic to use the brick factory. But fourthly as a factor in determining when the murder operation occurred is, Mladic says he's going to screen the men for war criminals. There is no screening done. Mladic flat out lied. No significant screening. They did not even minimally keep IDs. IDs were piled up and burned. If you were screening, you would need to get the IDs of the men so you could identify who were men of interest and who were men that could be released. Once they go to Batkovic, they're going to be registered by the ICRC and you're going to lose them. So if you truly want to screen them and be able to get people in order to -- God only knows what would happen to them, probably the same thing that happened at Palic. But you need to make lists. You should interrogate them. None of that happened in any significant way. This is the factor that you can rely on and you can bank to show that this murder operation was in play, had been decided by the afternoon of 12 July because we see no screening. In addition, the men are treated less than animals. There's little, little water, just enough to keep them alive. No food, no first aid. They're kept in horrendous conditions. Worse than animals. You wouldn't treat an animal that way. They were clearly marked for death. All right. So that brings us to the next critical phase. On the 13th of July, thousands of prisoners, at least 1.000, appear on the road at Kasaba in the morning. These are men that are turning themselves in, as we know. Is Tolimir involved in that? Does he know about that, like he has with every other group of prisoners or potential prisoners? Yes, absolutely. And we know that because even though he is in Zepa that -- beginning on the morning of the 13th, we have a document, a now-famous document, and I want you to see that document, it's Exhibit P125. This is the document authored by Savcic, talking about a proposal that General Tolimir made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think this document is confidential. It should not be broadcast. No, it was a mistake. I was misled. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's good to have caution. You will recall this as the document from the very beginning the Defence has challenged its authentic. They said it's a fake. They said it in their trial brief, they said it during trial. They said it in their closing brief. They repeatedly challenged it. This is a fake. But let's see what it is. We know from the testimony of General Savcic that he and Tolimir in the morning are in Borike and that there's discussion over the telephone with Malinic who's in Kasaba. We have intercept to that fact, about these men that are appearing in large numbers in Kasaba and that this is a topic of discussion between Tolimir and Savcic. Despite the fact that Zepa is due to start on the 14th, Tolimir is completely involved in this and receiving detailed information on it. We know that. Whenever you see a Tolimir document, don't forget it's basing information that he has received. It's not just a one-way street. He doesn't send out these proposals unless he gets the material. We don't have -- we only have a fraction of the material in this case. So he is getting quite a bit of information. Look at the proposal. It's to the commander of the Main Staff, Mladic, and for the information of General Gvero and the commander of the military police who was Malinic. And it's "order." So this is an order. And then it leads with a factual background about the thousand members of the former 28th Division that are in the area of Kasaba and under the control of the MP battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment of the Main Staff. And then it says -- Savcic says: "Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the GSVRS proposes the following measures ..." And then he lists the four proposals, all of which have to do with secrecy, normal secrecy to hide the operation that's going on. But what has always been considered abnormal was this fourth proposal: "Once the commander of the Military Police Battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff" -- I'm sorry, I've got the wrong one. I meant 3. "The commander of the Military Police Battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the Main Staff Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or air." Now, Savcic told us - as we knew otherwise - that the only people who had access to the air in the daytime was NATO. And so this is a deliberate attempt to hide these large number of prisoners from NATO. And why would they want to do that? Mladic has told Nesib Mandzic early that he had a choice: If they surrendered, they could survive; if they did not, they could disappear. Now, this is Tolimir's effort to be consistent with Mladic's order and make them disappear. We asked Savcic to give us an interpretation of what this would be about. He didn't say it was authentic, he didn't say it was not authentic. And when first asked about this, his explanation was: Well, we would have been concerned that NATO would have thought that this large group of people were, in fact, Serbs and would bomb them. I mean, this is so absurd that this clearly goes to the consciousness of General Savcic, knowing that this is an inculpatory document and he's doing his best under questioning to get away from the truth. That's exactly what General Tolimir's continued allegation that this is a fake is all about. If this is just a document trying to keep military issues secret, why isn't it said so early on and frequently, by Savcic, by Tolimir, by anyone? It's not. The one thing you got finally in the trial brief: Oh, if you believe this isn't a fake, well then it doesn't mean anything anyway. There's nothing wrong about it. Well, you can't unring that bell. You can't call this document a fake over and over and over again and ignore the key evidence of a soldier, Danko Gojkovic, who recognised his handwriting and said that this kind of document is the kind of thing he sent. I won't go over all the evidence with you, how genuine this document is. It's immense. We found another document in this collection that was by the same typewriter, the same typewritten. So someone somehow faked two documents, somehow placed them in the Drina Corps collection that we ended up finding, or we faked it. I mean, it's absurd as a lot of their Defence case is full of conspiracy theories and false allegations. This document, this proposal is a significant contribution to the murder operation to keep it secret, to keep it quiet, everything says that, all the factors in this case lead to that conclusion. Now, Butler, if you may recall, felt that the order to put them indoors came from Savcic. However, the four proposals of Tolimir, this is proposal number 3, so in any event, as Mr. Butler said, this document is a joint effort of Tolimir and Savcic to hide those prisoners pursuant to the murder operation. All right. The second known contribution of General Tolimir on the 13th or perhaps the 14th was when Tolimir, having remembered, if you recall, going up to Bijeljina to prepare them for the 1.000 to 1200 prisoners, when Todorovic calls Tolimir and says: Where are these people coming? He first told us he did this within about 24 hours of Tolimir arranging it, and since Tolimir arranged it on the 12th that's about the 13th, maybe 48, so the 13th or the 14th. But it's absolutely clear, Todorovic was clear as a bell, he calls Tolimir because the families of people, Serbs relatives that are in custody desperately want prisoners so that they can be exchanged. This is a huge issue that -- if you remember that Todorovic's commander is worried about and so they call. You don't make preparations for a thousand people and sit around for days wondering when they're going to be there. So he calls Tolimir and he speaks to Tolimir and Tolimir says: "It's not going to happen. Drop all further preparations. This idea has been given up on." This means General Tolimir knows that those prisoners are no longer going to the ICRC camp at Batkovic. He must know about the murder operation. He has to know their fate by this time. And remember, when Todorovic calls 13th, perhaps the 14th, he tried to stretch it on to the 15th, Tolimir clearly will have known about this before Todorovic called because Tolimir was the one who was so personally involved in getting to Batkovic, he has to be told and informed and involved in the decision not to send them to Batkovic. And if you recall, the decision to send people to Zvornik was made the afternoon/evening of the 13th of July. In fact, the first group went up on the 13th of July to Zvornik. So there's no way that by the evening, early evening of 13 of July when the VRS has decided to send people to Zvornik to be executed, they have not told General Tolimir. It was his job to get them to Batkovic, now they're going to their death in Zvornik, he has to be told. So by the evening of 13 July there's no doubt now that General Tolimir is fully aware and engaged, he's still in communications, he's still the top man of intel and security. He's at Borike. They even have a line to Boksanica by the 14th of July. So the next critical phase happens later that evening. First we have the afternoon when the thousand show up. Surprise enough. By the evening it's now, according to the VRS intercept and rough records 5- to 6.000 people in that area. Now, remember they started the killing on the morning of the 13th of July at the Jadar River where they had an execution squad and a bus load of people pulled away from the transportation operation of the women deliberately to kill people along the road. That kind of thing does not happen without the command's involvement. And then later in the day around 5.00 or 5.30, they murder a thousand people at the Kravica warehouse. And so by the time we have the evening come around there's 6.000 people, 5- to 6.000 people that need to be put indoors. People are dead at the Jadar River, they're lying dead in the Kravica warehouse. Is Tolimir aware of this? Does he know that thousands show up? Absolutely. Absolutely he does. We know that. And remember, they've tried killing people at Jadar, they've tried killing people at -- or they have killed people, they've killed people at Kravica, but now they have not 1500 to 2.000, they've got 6.000 people, and there's internationals going up and down that road. DutchBat is still trying to get to Kladanj, ICRC, MSF, UNMOs, these people are in Bratunac, these people are in Potocari, the world is focused on that particular area. They've got 5.000 people. They've got this huge issue. They've got to get them out of there. We see this. At this critical juncture look at Deronjic again. Deronjic is trying to get the Milici people to take these folks. Milici won't have anything to do with it. Beara wants to keep them in Bratunac and kill them. There is a huge fight between Deronjic and Beara on that point. Remember the intercept between Karadzic and Deronjic, where Karadzic is saying get those people out in warehouses outside. That's clearly the thousands that they're talking about. And they finally decide as Beara sends Momir up to Zvornik that they get them to Zvornik. Well, is Tolimir engaged in this controversy, in this critical decision on how to best dispose of these 6.000 live people that they can't possibly murder in Bratunac? Of course he is. He's been made aware of every other movement of prisoners, so of course he is and we know absolutely. The Defence acknowledges this because of the next document. This is a document. I don't think you need to see it, but it's late night, the 13th of July, and it's a document that as you recall security officer from Rogatica Carkic said he took his dictation from Tolimir. There's no way they could call that a fake. And it's Tolimir's proposal to move 800 people from the Kasaba area down to Sjemec to do farm work. Now, you heard from the logistics officer Radzulac [phoen]. There was no farm work to be done in that area at that time of year. That was nonsense. That was Tolimir's internal covering himself and covering him, which he did frequently. You'll see plenty of documents, oh, there's the -- we'll get to the famous September document where he criticises the VRS for not taking enough prisoners knowing all the prisoners that were taken by the Drina Corps. He throws in the Geneva Conventions when he doesn't mean it. Well, this was an internal security designation to hide his true intention, basically move 800 people secretly down to Rogatica to try to relieve the burden off of Zvornik and Bratunac and to enter into this. It's personally to Gvero, so -- and remember Jadar River at this time, dead, Kravica, dead. Probably a hundred people around the Vuk Karadzic school, dead, and who is implementing this but Beara, Salapura, Jankovic, Popovic, all the whole security branches. So by the evening, late evening of 13 July when Tolimir admittedly sends this document down, he is fully engaged. And this document -- we're -- we -- I wouldn't be surprised if we found a mass grave down there some day, but we do not have any evidence that this proposal was taken up on. But that is planning. It's part of the planning process, when senior officers make proposals to do people, to do things, it's part of the planning, it's pursuant to the murder operation. Whether the 800 are designed to be killed or not, he knows the rest are going to be killed. And all the 800 were killed. But this is where it gets absurd. Of course he knows and he's engaged and he's writing about it and he's receiving information on it. The Defence's explanation for this is that: Oh, this is just him making his effort to give them adequate accommodations or some such thing. I mean, you saw those awful Kravica -- worse than Kravica warehouse-like buildings, barely good enough for animals, if that, and that's exactly the kind of place people were stored and butchered. Tolimir got intel from Carkic or the commander and was able to fill that in. He says in his brief: Oh, no, it's not those places, it's the houses along the road. 800 people are going to fit in those houses? This is absurd. I'm surprised they even suggested as much. All right. The next critical phase now that by the evening of the 13th a decision's been made, everyone's going to Zvornik. The next day is the first day for the Zepa attack. Tolimir is there. He's at Borike, he's overseeing it. Now Krstic remembers commanding that attack, so Tolimir is not an active combat commander, no one's ever said he was, but he is there. What is one of the first things he does? Does it have to do with Zepa? No, it's Srebrenica. Exhibit P124 is a document that he sends out to the Drina Corps saying: We have received information that unmanned aircraft are flying above the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves. The next exhibit is P128, and he sends it to the Bratunac Brigade, the Zvornik Brigade, all Drina Corps Brigades, and it's an order to shoot down that unmanned aircraft that is recording. Well, what's going on up there around Srebrenica on the morning of the 14th that Tolimir would know about? Now, militarily the Bratunac Brigade is going through the woods, mopping up, trying to find any remaining Muslims. Is this going to be seen from the air? No. Men running around in the woods like that. But what else is happening, there's a huge convoy containing 5- 6.000 men that's gearing up and driving off to Bratunac the morning of the 14th. Also the morning of the 14th they're finishing off people at the Kravica warehouse, bringing in bulldozers, scraping the remains of the people up, and making a big pit at Glogova. Also, you've seen yourself that that can be seen from the air. And of course we know what goes on in Zvornik that day at Orahovac. So Tolimir's order to shoot down this plane that is recording images over the killing fields is a significant contribution to the murder operation. He knows unquestionably that this is happening, and despite that this is the first day of the attack he's still focused on Srebrenica. And this is the tip of the iceberg. What other information he's getting? Now, at this period of time which, just to remind you, our critical point was the job of secretly executing and burying thousands of prisoners as soon as possible 14 through 16 July. He issues the order to shoot down the unmanned aircraft. We don't hear from him much after that, but we know that Beara, Popovic, the whole, the security branch, Salapura, are organising and implementing the murder operations in Zvornik, Orahovac, at Petkovci during this time. And there is a document, I won't put it up on the screen, it's an exhibit in the case that shows all the security branch personnel at all the crime scenes during these days, and Beara is leading it from the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade and is on the ground, Popovic is all over the place, as are Nikolic and Trbic, Tolimir is leading it from Zepa. The other thing I won't spend a lot of time on but on the 14th Tolimir is within communications, and we know from the evidence that on the -- earlier on the 14th of July, Salapura called the Zvornik Brigade duty officer and left a message that Drago and Beara are to report to Golic, that's got to be Drago Nikolic. We know who Beara is. Pavle Golic is the intel officer at the Drina Corps in Vlasenica who is co-ordinating communications of the murder operation. So there's no way Salapura is passing on messages to Beara without Salapura being involved in the murder operation. Clearly we know Beara and Drago are. And information is being focused on Golic at the Drina Corps Brigade, which in turn goes of course to the Main Staff, and Tolimir has access to the Main Staff information at all times from where he is. That's been clear. We spent a lot of time on that in the brief and you'll see the communications show that. Salapura says he doesn't remember this call but he doesn't contest it. He suggests he received the information from Mladic but he says it should have gone through the staff, meaning of course Tolimir. On the evening of the 14th of July, the Zvornik Brigade receives a call and a messages that Beara is to call 155. So the evening of all these mass executions going on in Orahovac and Petkovci, there's a call to call 155, and I'm sure you remember 155 is the line that is picked up by the operations room in the Main Staff. This is a room that Tolimir is imminently familiar with, can access from Borike, from Boksanica, from Rogatica, from the forward command post at Krivace. He's also got portable radios that he's called in. This is where the hub of information now is and Beara is having to report, naturally. Beara is the subordinate of Tolimir. Tolimir suggests merely that Beara is -- that he does not oversee Beara, that he does not command Beara. He just says it with no backup. Completely disregards the testimony of Obradovic and Milovanovic who clearly establish that as the top man of intel and security Tolimir is the commander of his staff, Beara, Salapura, Jankovic as the other assistant commanders are the commanders of their staff. They are not military combat commanders but they are commanders, they have the right to order, they're responsible for the work of those people. They don't deal with that at all. Maybe we'll hear something today about that. They make this bold conclusion, but then it's completely contradicted by all the evidence. All right. Number 6, the critical event that's now occurring over the period of 14 and 15 July is that the job of executing 1500 prisoners in Pilica has been delayed. They've had to spend the nights of 14th and 15th in Pilica without men to execute them. Remember we have Beara at the Zvornik Brigade calling Zivanovic first and then calling Krstic and trying to get men that Mladic had ordered to come to the execution sites. That's because they were able to kill the people at Orahovac on the 14th. The night of the 15th they killed the people at Petkovci. The day of the 15th they killed the people at Rocevic, at Kozluk. But the 15th goes by with nobody of the 1500 men that are rotting literally in the Pilica school and the Pilica dom. They are going on their second night, the night of the 15th, in this squalor unexecuted, and Beara is fit to be tied as you can tell by looking at that. Why doesn't Beara call his commander, his boss, Tolimir? Well, Tolimir is not a military commander, he does not control troops. Tolimir can get on the line to Krstic or Mladic and say that the commander has ordered you get it to them, but it's easier for Beara who's in the Zvornik Brigade to go directly to the Drina Corps and get Zivanovic and Krstic who are commanders who do have the right to control troops, that's why he goes there. But of course Tolimir is going to be abreast of this. Mladic is in Belgrade. This needs to be -- happen. Every day that 1500 men go without it being executed is a day longer that this thing could be exposed. So this is a very, very difficult situation they are facing. You remember that Pilica official comes down and complains to the Zvornik Brigade. It's a mess. Who do they get to solve this problem? The 10th Sabotage Detachment, controlled by the intel section, Salapura, who's controlled by Tolimir. Of course Tolimir was -- gave his approval for the 10th Sabotage, fully aware and in the know of it. Mladic is -- it's Mladic's unit, of course, but it's controlled and dealt with by Tolimir. Mladic doesn't have time to deal with the units that he's dealing with. Mladic is in Belgrade. Of course Tolimir was informed of this. Something this major, this big a problem has to take precedence for Tolimir, and the 10th Sabotage for his people, they get sent over and they do the job on the 16th. Also on the 16th the Main Staff orders the Drina Corps to continue the murders at Pilica. Remember, we have an intercept, Cerovic, probably the duty officer at the Drina Corps, says to Beara that Trkulja, the Main Staff officer, I think, for artillery, Trkulja was just here and wants triage to be -- and is passing on from above that triage needs to be done on the prisoners in Pilica. Then we have the intercept where Beara and Cerovic get on the phone and Cerovic is telling Beara this. Beara says don't talk about it over the phone. So we have Trkulja coming from the Main Staff on the 16th telling the Drina Corps to get -- make sure those prisoners are killed. Tolimir has full access to the Main Staff and the information, and in fact I'm sure is co-ordinating it and the efforts of his subordinates on the 16th. Later on in the evening Tolimir goes to Crna Rijeka. We know this from Keserovic, and this is critical testimony because Keserovic gave us a statement early on before really understanding how it was going to be used. Tolimir is there, Mladic is there, and according to Keserovic, Tolimir is advising him and talking with Mladic about reducing Keserovic's task and going to command troops for a sweep operation in Bratunac the next day. Well, what does that mean? The evening of 16 July, 7.000 Muslims are almost dead, I'm sure hundreds are still dying of their wounds on the killing fields of Branjevo and in the squalor of the Pilica dom, but there is Mladic and Tolimir at Crna Rijeka, and Tolimir - there's no question - is briefing Mladic on what's happening. Tolimir has to know what's gone on, he's got the information from the Main Staff, the ops room, he's gotten from the Drina Corps. He's briefing Mladic. It's a critical contribution to the murder operation. He's also briefing Keserovic on how to deal with Jankovic who he knows is in Bratunac. But very importantly, remember Keserovic said to us: Oh, Tolimir told me Beara was in the Drina zone. In the interview which is in evidence, Keserovic said Tolimir told us Beara was at the Drina Corps headquarters. So Tolimir is not only briefing Keserovic on what Jankovic is up to, he's briefing them on Beara. The man that they won't even talk about. Another outrageous point in the brief. Oh, Beara. We're not going to talk about Beara, Naval Captain Beara, as if the fact that he's a naval captain means something. Here is direct evidence that Tolimir is aware that Beara is in the heart of darkness on the Vlasenica Brigade on the key night of the 16th when people are dead and dying all over Pilica. And they're thinking about killing these poor MSF workers. I won't go through all the detail on that. But I refer to that. It's part 7 is the -- the job post-16 July, what to do with the Muslim men in Bratunac and who should be executed and who should not be. I'll merely remind you of the documents Jankovic wrote explaining this problem, what do we do with the MSF and that amazing and outrageous intercept where Djurdjic, the person who deals with internationals, says to Jankovic over the phone, Well, are they able-bodied? Well, yes. He goes, Well, you know what they procedure was, you were in Bratunac the previous days, and they get into an argument about it. And it ends with wait until Toso gets there. He's the commander. He'll decide. It's about the third reference to Tolimir being involved in this whole situation where MSF become involved. So they're clearly going through Toso, Tolimir, for these issues. This again is part of the planning even though thank God these MSF workers were not killed, Tolimir was involved in the planning and in the discussions on their fate and very smartly decides not to kill them because it's his job to keep this thing secret. You go and kill 15 MSF workers that were sitting with DutchBat and this organisation and ICRC, I mean, it really makes things obvious. Tolimir had to put the lid on that and I'm sure he did. All right. Point 8, the job to receive, transport, and kill 30 or more Muslims captured in Serbia and return to Popovic on the 22nd/23rd of July. You'll remember the documents and the material showing that people tried to escape to Serbia and got grabbed and sent back. There was Muslims that actually cut themselves to try to stay. They were given through the Bratunac Brigade to Popovic, and on the 23rd of July Popovic got the 10th Sabotage and murdered them. On the 22nd of July Popovic does something unusual, it was stupid, insecure, he gets on an insecure line and he calls Tolimir directly. The only reason he was stupid enough to do this was because it was a family issue. He had a cousin that was captured and he wanted to go directly to Tolimir to get the information. But in that conversation he says, Oh, I'm doing work. Yeah, this is the work he's doing. He's about ready to butcher 30 people and he's gone over to the Zvornik Brigade that day, and I believe that's when he picks up the Milici patients. So Popovic is a very busy guy and there's only one thing he's doing and that's killing people. Tolimir tells him: Keep up the work or something to that effect, Tolimir fully engaged with the knowledge of this operation now. Knows precisely what Popovic is doing and issues him the comment: Keep doing your work. This is another clear contribution. Number 9, the job to continue to hide and cover up the murder operation and the continued murders. Those murders as they are charged in the indictment are Nezuk, Snagovo. Those two are people that get captured, just a small number, and they get shot by the soldiers that are there. No real reason to believe that Tolimir is going to be aware of that or in on those particular small-level murders, but that is a clear indication that the murder operation, if they can get away with killing people they will and they do. The evidence on Nezuk and Snagovo is clear. The Milici patients, some 10 to 15 seriously injured patients. I bring them up because if you look at the documents and how they got transferred from Milici to the Zvornik to the Zvornik Brigade to Popovic on the 23rd, the Main Staff medical officer was involved in the approving of that transfer. To murder seriously injured patients that had been seen by two hospitals and are still alive on the 23rd is an outrageous decision that could only have been made at the highest levels. Mladic and Tolimir, they have to know about that. The four Branjevo farm survivors, as you recall, the four folks that were helped by the two Serb soldiers, given an apple and sandwich and told where the front lines were. Then they were captured and confessed that they were helped by these two Serbs. Well Drago Nikolic, Vinko Popovic, General Tolimir prosecuted those two Serb soldiers for helping the enemy, and they used the statements of those four guys to prosecute them and punish them. And those four guys, we have their names, have never been seen since. They got murdered. They're part of the official record of that case. There's no way that happened. That kind of thing does not happen without a green light given to it at the highest level. I don't know if he knew about that in particular. But it's just -- it's the kind of thing that his army was doing throughout this time-period. The Skorpions were a unit that were working with the MUP in Trnovo. The MUP was under the command of the army. The MUP were working with the MUP -- sorry, the Skorpions were working with -- it was Borovcanin outfit, actually. They send Srebrenica victims all the way across Bosnia and then they're murdered by the Serbian MUP unit who happens to be working with the VRS and RS forces. There's no way you send that many people across the country to be murdered by a foreign unit or a unit from the Republika Krajina without the Main Staff knowing and without Tolimir knowing. Mr. Elderkin will talk about Palic. People were killed in the woods. There's one document that's particularly disturbing. It's P00755, it's a daily combat report of Rajko Kusic. And in that he basically says: Today we liquidated several Muslims and from them we learned the following, and then he gives their location and what they were doing. They clearly captured people, got information from them, and then murdered them, and then reported that up the chain to the Drina Corps command. Talk about impunity. This kind of thing does not happen unless it's part of the ongoing process of the Drina Corps and of the Main Staff. Now, that brings me to an end of my ten critical points. I could talk about the other issues, the other factors involved, but I wanted to be able to tell that to you in a compact form as it's been in my head all these years. And as you go over this material and think about it and understand it, please don't forget: This army is working, it's working according to the chain of command. Tolimir is at its head, he's fully engaged even from Zepa, he is involved. Now, I think it's a good time to take a break. We'll get Mr. Vanderpuye here. I hope to have just a few minutes at the end to wrap this up or perhaps we can wait for the rebuttal which you have kindly offered us, but if we could take the break now, Mr. President, it would be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. We will have our first break now and resume with a submission by Mr. Vanderpuye after the break at five minutes past 4.00. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye. Welcome to the courtroom. As we heard from Mr. McCloskey, it's now your turn to present the views of the Prosecution. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very kindly, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Gajic and to you, General Tolimir and everyone. Your Honours, it's my privilege to appear before you today to present part of the Prosecution's closing submissions in this very serious and obviously historically important case. As the Chamber is aware, the accused is charged with responsibility for the crimes alleged in the indictment under Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute and under each mode of liability including joint criminal enterprise. In his closing brief, aside from basically acknowledging his position as the VRS Main Staff's assistant commander for security and intelligence during the war, General Tolimir has acknowledged little else. He has challenged essentially every material aspect of this case, including the crime base evidence, ranging from the number of Srebrenica dead and missing to the very nature of the Muslim population's removal from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. It is clearly General Tolimir's right to put the Prosecution to proof, and of course we recognise and accept that the burden of proof in this case is ours alone. We are nevertheless confident that on the record of these proceedings, General Tolimir's involvement and guilt in the horrendous and unspeakable crimes charged in the indictment is proved beyond any reasonable doubt. Except to underscore and highlight some of the core issues establishing General Tolimir's individual criminal responsibility and to respond to specific assertions that are made in the Defence closing brief, I will to the greatest extent possible try to refrain from restating matters that are extensively addressed in the Prosecution's final brief. Instead, I'll focus on two salient aspects of General Tolimir's responsibility. First, following on from my colleague Mr. McCloskey's submissions, I'll address the facts and circumstances proving General Tolimir's significant contributions to the murder JCE by means of his omissions. Second, I'll address the key facts proving the JCE to forcibly transfer the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa and General Tolimir's full participation in it. General Tolimir's failure to protect the Muslim prisoners in VRS custody following Srebrenica's fall was a serious violation of international law, and there is no question about that. On the evidence in this case, the fact of his failure is not complicated nor is it particularly nuanced; to the contrary, it is stark, it is glaring, it is unassailable, and it is undeniable. General Tolimir's omissions were no less a significant contribution to the JCE to murder the men and boys of Srebrenica than his positive conduct which you've just heard about. Like his positive actions, the omissions were the product of a conscious choice and demonstrate his commitment to achieving the criminal objectives of the JCE, and for this reason they too give rise to his responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Tribunal's Statute. To be clear, indictment paragraph 29(D) alleges General Tolimir's responsibility for failing to protect the Muslim prisoners and it provides specifically that he had responsibility for the handling of all of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners taken after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave and to ensure their safety and welfare and he failed to do so. Your Honours, the evidence in this case bears this out. First, General Tolimir had a duty under customary international law to ensure the humane treatment and protection of the Muslim prisoners in VRS custody, especially those within the custody of the organs, units, and officers over which or whom General Tolimir exercised control. As explained in the Prosecution's closing brief under the Geneva Convention III, all agents of a detaining power, in this case the Republika Srpska, having custody of prisoners have a duty to ensure their humane treatment, and that duty applies to individuals including those with direct custody of prisoners and those individuals who supervise them. Given his position, there is no question that General Tolimir was an agent of the detaining power. He was a member of the VRS, of the Main Staff of the VRS, and the duty to protect applied to him. Second, and equally clear, Tolimir supervised many of the officers in whose custody the Muslim men and boys taken prisoner following the collapse of the enclave -- Srebrenica enclave and then later Zepa found themselves. These officers included Ljubisa Beara, colonel, chief of the security administration of the Main Staff; Dragomir Pecanac, who I'm sure you remember, was an intelligence officer within General Tolimir's sector; Vujadin Popovic, who my colleague's just referred to was the chief of security of the Drina Corps; Momir Nikolic, the chief of intelligence and security of the Bratunac Brigade; Drago Nikolic, the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade; Milorad Trbic, another security officer and Drago Nikolic's assistant in the Zvornik Brigade; Zoran Carkic; as well as Bratunac Brigade MPs including Mirko Jankovic; Zvornik Brigade MPs including Milomir Jasikovac, and that's just to name a few. That General Tolimir "commanded," and I say this in quotes, "commanded" Ljubisa Beara, his immediate subordinate within the security and intelligence sector who was a key figure in the planning and implementation of the murder operation is amply established by the evidence in this case, and it is not in doubt that General Tolimir maintained professional control over the VRS military police and the subordinate security organs which included officers having custody over the Muslim prisoners. It was General Tolimir's sector that was responsible for the training and equipping and guiding subordinate security organs, sabotage units including the 10th Sabotage Unit and the military police within the VRS, and indeed it was his sector that was responsible for dealing with prisoner issues such as their interrogation and their securing. The legality and correctness of the work of a subordinate security officers and organs were General Tolimir's exclusive responsibility. You will find that in P1112, page 3, item 7. A number of documents in evidence further establish General Tolimir's active exercise of authority over subordinate security organs, personnel, and the military police. These documents show, for instance, his issuance of assignments and orders. An example is P2430 and that's a Main Staff document where he reports on the combat-readiness and issues assignments to the 65th Regiment Protection military police. There's another document which is P2141 in which he is enforcing a prior order for subordinate units to submit names so that the Main Staff can establish the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And other documents such as the promulgation and dissemination of rules and guide-lines, in particular concerning the treatment of prisoners. An example of that is P1970. Remember that Tolimir's security and intelligence subordinates and the military police were directly engaged in the events in Potocari, in Bratunac, in Zvornik, and in fact they were involved in every single phase of the murder operation. They had, without question, custody and control over the prisoners at every stage. They detained them, they secured them, they questioned them, they transported them, and in the end they were the ultimate instrumentality of their extermination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please slow down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you heard the comment. Please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll do, Mr. President. There is no real contest about whether General Tolimir was under a duty to protect the Muslim prisoners, particularly as one in a supervisory position over the VRS officers and units in whose custody the prisoners were. Similarly, General Tolimir's knowledge of the VRS custody of these prisoners is not an issue. You'll recall, and I believe my colleague has just reminded the Chamber, of a 12th July document in which General Tolimir is directing that fleeing Muslims be arrested and detained. You recall the document that my colleague referred to, I think it was P122, 13 July document, referring to the thousand prisoners in Dusan Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you again. It's very difficult to listen when we hear the sound of typing at the same time because of the -- it's from the same table. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Aside from the document which the Defence has disputed in their brief, the testimony in the evidence of General Savcic who was with General Tolimir on 13 July in the morning establishes that General Tolimir was put on notice of the numbers of prisoners that were surrendering at Dusan Nova Kasaba through a telephone call or a series of telephone calls that General Savcic received from Zoran Malinic, the head of the 65th Protection Military Police Battalion. Further evidence of General Tolimir's knowledge of the numbers of prisoners can be found in the 13 July document that he issued on the evening of 13 July requesting or proposing that 800 prisoners be sent down to the Sjemec farm in Rogatica. He also communicated with Milenko Todorovic, the chief of security of the East Bosnia Corps, advising him to prepare or take steps to prepare the Batkovic prison camp to receive a thousand to 1300 prisoners. He knew that there were thousands of prisoners by 13 July in VRS hands and he knew that they were going to be killed. Leaving aside the ample evidence of his direct involvement in the planning and implementation of these executions as my colleague has just detailed, the evidence in this case leaves no room for the Defence's fanciful suggestion that General Tolimir could not reasonably foresee the prisoners' exposure to grave harm in VRS custody and at any point during the ten-day period over which they were slaughtered. I say again "the ten-day period" because we start on the 13th of July by the Jadar River and we end up on the 23rd of July in Bisina. And in that time some 7.000 individuals were summarily executed with the involvement of the security and intelligence sector and their subordinates. Given the pervasive and sustained involvement of the security administration in perpetrating these crimes, nothing short of an army-wide, and in fact nation-wide, conspiracy to hide this information from General Tolimir could support his claimed ignorance of the grossly criminal acts and conduct of his immediate and professional subordinates throughout this unmitigated bloodletting. The serious mistreatment of Muslim prisoners in VRS custody was rampant and it was known. The Chamber will recall the evidence of the opportunistic killings in Bratunac and in Potocari. You saw the video footage of the Kravica warehouse from 13 July with bodies strewn all over the ground there. The executions that happened -- those executions, rather, happened within hours of General Tolimir sending his proposal to send 800 prisoners down to Rogatica. On 14 July bodies were being buried at Glogova, as arranged by Tolimir's immediate subordinate Ljubisa Beara. That day Beara and Popovic and Nikolic, all three security officers together with the military police, organised and transported thousands of Muslim prisoners to the Zvornik area, implementing their plan to exterminate them. You heard from Tanacko Tanic, he was a member of the Zvornik Brigade command, and he told you that the murders up at Kozluk on the 15th could be seen from across the Drina River. He also made this key observations, and it's rather astute in its frankness. He says: "These killings were taking place in populated areas. People saw this, people had phones." The VRS had phones too. They had radios, they had teleprinters, they had couriers. This didn't happen in the Stone Age; it happened in 1995, and the suggestion that the highest intelligence officer in the Main Staff of the VRS and the highest organ of the VRS was in the dark because he wasn't physically at the locations where these crimes occurred, at the locations where his colleagues were perpetrating these crimes, crimes committed on an unprecedented scale, on an arrestive scale in this war insults the intelligence. These were crimes that involved his very subordinates from the battalion level to the brigade level to the corps level and to the Main Staff level, virtually every level of the VRS organisational structure under his direction. These are crimes that could easily have jeopardised the Bosnian Serb war effort and they did and they were crimes of a scale, as I say, in many ways unparalleled throughout the war. What the evidence proves in this case, Your Honours, beyond any reasonable doubt is that with knowledge that thousands of Muslim men and boys were in VRS custody, with knowledge that they were to be harmed, at least harmed gravely, and in this case murdered, and with knowledge that his own subordinates and others were directly and actively involved in planning, organising, and executing their deaths in the most brutal and systematic, sustained, and callous way, Tolimir failed absolutely to ensure their protection. These omissions directly and at least significantly contributed to the success of the murder operation and ensured its successful planning, it ensured its successful organisation, and ensured that it could be carried out unimpeded and in fact professionally implemented and run by members of the security and intelligence sector of which General Tolimir was concededly in charge. Tolimir had the material ability to act to protect these prisoners. He was one of General Mladic's most trusted assistant commanders. He was part of General Mladic's inner core, as he put it. Not only as a senior officer and as a general, but as a security official General Tolimir had a specific obligation under the VRS military rules - and these are rules of the security service and the constitution and laws of the Republika Srpska. I'm not going to go into too much detail here because a lot of this is covered in the brief, but in essence the rules of service for security officers applied in the VRS and required General Tolimir to detect and prevent acts committed within the VRS as well as those outside of them. I stress within the VRS because these are the circumstances of this case. He was required to act in that way with respect to any act carried out in the VRS which subverted the constitutional order which is described in evidence in this case, and you have it in this case, and concerns the guarantee of and protection of human freedom and rights with respect to international standards. That's what it says in Article 5. It ostensibly assured national equality and protected the rights of ethnic groups, including Muslims. It ostensibly provided for the inviolability of life and protection from cruel and inhumane treatment. His job, his core competency was to prevent the violation of those guarantees. In that capacity, his responsibilities required him under VRS rules - not international rules - VRS rules for him to discover, prevent, report, arrest, and investigate the perpetrators and the accomplices of crimes against humanity in international law including those committed within the VRS, precisely the types of crimes that are alleged here. So the question is: What would have happened if General Tolimir had done any of this before or during the course of the murder operation? What would have happened if General Tolimir decided to act to actually protect the prisoners? If he took an action to arrest the planners of these crimes or the organisers of these crimes or the perpetrators of these crimes? If he investigated the issues? If he reported them? If he withdrew members of his sector and subordinates from participating in the plan? I think the answer's pretty clear, and that is: There's no way that these murders could have occurred and certainly not on the scale in which they were perpetrated. General Tolimir chose not to take an action for one reason and one reason only and that is because he was a part of it and because he intended to bring about the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise to murder the Muslim men and boys of Srebrenica. It was his intention through his omission to ensure that the murder operation was carried out efficiently. It was his intention to ensure that the murder operation was carried out undetected. It was his intention to simply make it happen, to implement the commander's orders like he's supposed to do as an assistant commander, and he did. As a career JNA officer, General Tolimir knew perfectly well that he had an obligation to ensure the humane treatment of prisoners, and this was not only as a result of his training but also because that duty was specifically codified in various army regulations. I will refer the Chamber to P2482, Article 210 which says: "Prisoners of war shall be treated humanely. In particular, they must be protected against violence, insults, and intimidation." Those are from the SFRY regulations on the application of the rules of international law of war. Protection from murder goes without saying. On the evidence in this case the fact that the murders of thousands of prisoners in VRS custody were planned, organised, and successfully implemented by members of the VRS Main Staff and VRS officers immediately proximate to the accused, whether his subordinates or not, and that General Tolimir chose not to take any action to protect those prisoners in accordance with his responsibilities under the VRS rules, the RS rules, the RS constitution, and international law all speak to his intent to achieve the objectives of those crimes. Keep in mind that given his long-standing involvement in prisoner exchange issues, his failure to act disregarded the VRS's own vested interests because it deprived them of the ability to use these prisoners for the purposes of exchange and for the purposes of extracting crucial and important intelligence information. As plain as day, the evidence in this case proves that General Tolimir's failure to act was deliberate, it was intentional, and can only have been calculated to further the criminal objectives of the murder JCE. They did that and he should be held fully to account for it. I would like to turn your attention if I could to the forcible transfer JCE. Notwithstanding the Defence's refusal to acknowledge that there was a JCE to forcibly remove the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa, the fact of its existence is proven beyond any reasonable doubt in this case. Proof of General Tolimir's unrelenting and substantial participation and contribution to this JCE is as clear as it is overwhelming. While the indictment alleges that the forcible transfer JCE began in March 1995, the underlying policy of the RS and VRS leadership to rid the eastern -- rid Eastern Bosnia of its Muslim inhabitants was in place much earlier, beginning with the implementation of the six strategic objectives. Other compelling evidence in this case establishes the criminal aims of the RS and VRS leadership to ethnically cleanse Serb-claimed territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the eastern enclaves. Remarkably the Defence argues that the six strategic objectives were put forward, and I quote, "as a kind of action plan." This is at paragraph 371 of the Defence closing brief. The evidence in this case of course proves that at the 16th Session of the RS National Assembly on 12 May 1992, these objectives were laid out, they were discussed, and they were fully embraced. Although their publication in the gazette in 1993 is anomalous, it is clear from the number that is assigned to the publication, which is 02-130/92, that the decision was taken in 1992, consistent with the declaration itself which attributes that to the 12th May 1992 Assembly Session. In any event, these war goals were clearly disseminated and implemented by the VRS. In his evidence, General Novica Simic, who is the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, recounted his 2nd September meeting, 1992, with Generals Mladic, Gvero, and Presidents Karadzic and Krajisnik, president of the RS National Assembly. At that meeting the strategic objectives were discussed and he wrote them down in his war diary. You have that evidence before you. You have his testimony at P2756 and you have the diary at P2752. The VRS Main Staff's 1992 analysis of combat-readiness, which is P2880, also refers expressly to the implementation of the strategic objectives. It talks about their progress, and this exposes of course the fallacy of the Defence's arguments. The 1992 combat report states in part: "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the commands and units, served as a general guide-line upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles." You'll find that in that exhibit, 2880, at page 159. The Defence's assertions concerning the circumstances under which the strategic objectives were decided fundamentally amount to nothing more than an unfortunate attempt to distract from the real issues in this case, those issues which unmistakably underpin General Tolimir's criminal responsibility for the forcible transfer of tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims in 1995. As noted in the Prosecution's brief, strategic objectives 1 and 3 culminated in the forcible transfer of the Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa. Strategic objective 1 called for, and I quote, "to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities." As General Simic noted down in his diary in shorthand: "Separation from the Muslims." Strategic objective number 3: "The elimination of the Drina River as a border between Serb states." This was implemented so as to remove the Muslim presence in Eastern Bosnia. Again General Simic wrote this down: "Drina River valley to Serbs." The 16th Assembly Session minutes confirm that interpretation and say: "That the belt along the Drina must basically belong to the Serbs." In addition, recall that operational directives issued at the Main Staff level were also implemented and in particular directive 4. That was issued on the 19th of November, 1992, and was an important step in the realisation of strategic objective number 3. Directive 4 expressed the RS leadership's policy of ethnic cleansing and put it in motion, and this policy was pursued by the VRS in Eastern Bosnia right through 1995. General Tolimir and the security and intelligence sector under his command had to have been involved in developing this directive which required the expertise and input of each assistant commander. Directive 4 ordered the Drina Corps to: "Force him," meaning the military, Bosnian Muslim military, "to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the ... Muslim population." Birac of course included Srebrenica. Given the gravity and the manifest implications of this language, it hardly comes as a surprise that a number of VRS officers have tried to explain it away. However, the candid evidence of Colonel Milenko Lazic, who was a Drina Corps operations and training officer who worked in the Main Staff from 1992 to 1993, puts things in perspective. Asked whether an objective of the VRS was to separate the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina by their ethnicity, he said this: You'll find this by the way at P2733, transcript lines are 21833 basically through to 21835. He says: "I think the main objective of the VRS was to defend the Serb population from the attacks coming from the other side. And if there was no other solution available, then to separate ... us on ethnic principles. And I believe that that was the understanding of every individual member of the VRS." If there was any ambiguity in directive 4's language, Milenko Zivanovic, the commander of the Drina Corps, the one responsible for implementing the tasks assigned to the Drina Corps under the directive makes things even clear.
