In issuing order 2-126 on 24 November 1992 implementing the tasks of directive number 4, he ordered: "Inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender." And I'll add this. Significantly and unambiguously he says: "Force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Confronted with this language you'll remember the Defence's so-called military expert. His explanation was: "I honestly don't know why" Zivanovic "put this sentence in this order in this manner." I would submit to the Chamber that there is one very obvious explanation and that is that the language reflects precisely what General, at the time Colonel, Zivanovic meant and it reflects precisely what directive 4 really called for, the separation along ethnic lines. On 4 July 1994 we see the Bratunac Brigade's then-commander Slavko Ognjenovic's report. He issued a report following General Mladic's briefing regarding the Corps's combat-readiness. In his report Ognjenovic says: "We must attain our final goal - an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task: The expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." If the language about making life unbearable and not surviving together with the rubric of disappearing and vanishing sounds familiar to the Chamber it's because it is and you've heard it countless times in the evidence of this case like a mantra. For instance, in August 1994 - and this is at P2228, it's a videotaped conversation with General Mladic and Milan Lesic who you recall was a Canadian supporter of the VRS and donor. As Mladic and Lesic are in the car driving towards the Zepa enclave you'll recall, Mladic says bluntly this: "Here you see, the Turks had blocked up all this. Here is the road to their village of Godjenje. Here is the village of Plane. It used to be Turkish. Now we will go towards it. You film this freely, you know, let our Serbs see what we have done to them, how we took care of the Turks. In Podrinje we thrashed the Turks. If the Americans and English, the Ukrainians and Canadians in Srebrenica - in the meantime it's the Dutch - would not protect them, they would have disappeared from this area long ago." Significantly in March 1995, seven months later, the supreme commander JCE member Radovan Karadzic issued directive number 7 and again we hear the mantra: Make the Muslims' lives unbearable. Drive them out. In assigning tasks to the Drina Corps directive 7 says: "By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And we are not talking about the army here. We are talking about regular people. We're talking about the whole of the Muslim population. The directive continues and says that: Relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our good will while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion. Astonishingly, or really perhaps not so astonishingly, the Defence claims that directive 7 was never implemented. They cite the fact that humanitarian aid convoys continued to come into the enclaves in support of this. However, indeed that was the point. The point was to strangle enclaves, allowing only so much in as would avoid international condemnation while at the same time bringing the populations in the enclaves to the breaking point. Obviously a complete cessation of aid into the enclaves would have assured international condemnation, it would have brought immediate action, and it would have defeated the directive's objective and exposed the pernicious plan behind it. In the end I suppose the Defence is left with no choice but to deny directive 7's implementation because it is nefarious - and that is clear on its face - and because the Main Staff had a direct involvement in its drafting, development, and implementation of which General Tolimir and his sector would have been a part. This would only crystallise the Main Staff and General Tolimir's participation in the realisation of the criminal objectives of directive 7. Again, Drina Corps commander Milenko Zivanovic dispels the Defence's vacuous contention that in fact detective 7 was replaced or superseded by detective 7/1 issued by General Mladic. In the Krivaja 95 attack order General Zivanovic specifically noted, and this is why the way P1202, he specifically noted that it was issued: "Pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff of the VRS." He took on the task of splitting apart the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and then reducing them to their urban areas. Obviously the reduction of the enclaves to their urban areas would all but guarantee a humanitarian disaster, forcing the surrounding civilian population into the concentrated urban areas of Srebrenica and Zepa would clearly have made life for the Muslim population unbearable and it did. Let me add that this order was not a secret. It was copied to the Main Staff and it was specifically approved by General Mladic. You'll see his signature recorded on the attack map and his approval of it. Given General Tolimir's crucial importance to Mladic and the Main Staff's decision-making and his involvement in the development of directive 7, Tolimir was fully informed of Krivaja 1995 including the operations. I'll talk about that a little bit more specifically in just a few minutes. There is no plausible debate about whether directive 7 was in fact implemented on the evidence of this case. The evidence proves that it was carried out in fact on its terms as calculated to create the conditions to force the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa, which contrary to the Defence position at paragraph 411 of their brief, the Bosnian Serb leadership clearly viewed as strategic. President Karadzic's speech at the 53rd National Assembly on 28 August 1995 crystallises this issue. And he says this: "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell you the truth, there are towns that we have grabbed for ourselves and there are only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give us the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours and no one is practically questioning it anymore." Tolimir was in attendance at this Assembly session and even addressed the Assembly. You have that in evidence at P2435. That there was a joint criminal enterprise to remove by force the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa is as certain in this case as the resultant crimes that you've seen. The Defence seems to argue in essence that the populations of Zepa and Srebrenica were not forcibly removed, but they left the enclave rather on their own accord or pursuant to an agreement. The evidence in this case presents precisely the opposite conclusion. I will not go into that much detail here either because I think it's quite well addressed in the Prosecution's closing brief. But the trial record is replete with evidence establishing that there was a forcible transfer and deportation of the Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa as well as the foreseeable crimes that occurred. I'm sure that the Chamber recalls the ample evidence of the shelling of civilian targets in the lead up to the attack on Srebrenica. You've heard from UNMOs, you've heard from victims, survivors, you've heard from other internationals such as DutchBat. You will recall, I'm sure, the terror attack that was carried out by the 10th Sabotage Detachment on 23 June 1995. The evidence of the relentless destruction of humanitarian -- a restriction, rather, of humanitarian convoys into the enclaves, the evidence of starvation and desperation within the Srebrenica population prior to the enclave's collapse, the fear and desperation of the Muslim population fleeing Srebrenica into Potocari from their homes and nearby villages as they were terrorised by Bosnian Serb forces, the deplorable and deteriorating conditions in Potocari which the crowd endured, a crowd of more than 20.000, 30.000 Muslim refugees, they endured for days prior to their expulsion from the enclaves. During that time on top of it, they were subjected to sniping attacks by VRS units. You will find that evidence in P598, transcript lines 2440 through 41 and transcript page 2486. I'm certain that the Chamber has not forgotten the video footage showing the despair and the fear on the faces of the women and children; and the men, the husbands, the brothers, the fathers, that were systematically torn away from as their families loaded onto waiting vehicles and kicked out of their homes. The Chamber, I'm sure, will recall the video footage of the events in Zepa where a virtual repeat of these events took place, where the population was shelled and forced into the hills and then forced back into the town and booted out on trucks and on buses, shipped off to Muslim-held areas. Or they were forced to flee on foot into Serbia, into the hands of the Serbian MUP in order to seek protection while Colonel Beara was arranging for them to be shot at as they crossed the Drina River in rafts, makeshift rafts, and you'll see that in the evidence, in the intercept evidence in this case, from August 2nd. The suggestion, as the Defence has advanced in this trial, that the populations of Srebrenica and Zepa left the enclaves on their own accord flies in the face of history, it flies in the face of reason, and it flies in the face of the overwhelming evidence, the overwhelming credible evidence in this case. Remember General Mladic's monologue at the Hotel Fontana when he said to Nesib Mandzic, a school teacher who was selected to meet with Mladic about the status of Muslim refugees in Potocari, and this is Exhibit P1008 which is the Prosecution's trial video, he says to Nesib Mandzic: "Have I made myself clear? Nesib, the future of your people is in your hands, not only in this territory" and he says "I am finished." "Bring the people who can secure the surrender of weapons and save your people from destruction." He says: "I need to have a clear position of the representatives of your people on whether you want to survive, stay, or vanish." You will find this at P1008, transcript reference page 47 through 48. Before General Mladic had his answer, because they adjourned that meeting to the next day, 10.00 a.m., 12 July, before he had his answer about whether or not that Muslim population wanted to stay, to survive, or to vanish, those buses were already rolling. Before the 10.00 a.m. meeting on the 12th when he repeated the mantra and as he says: "As I told this gentleman last night, you can survive or you can disappear," those buses were already on the ground rolling. They were already on their way to take those Muslims out of the enclave. At 12.50 on the 12th of July General Mladic was intercepted saying this: "They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to." General Tolimir was one of Mladic's closest advisors. He was in the inner core, as General Mladic said. He was part of the decision-making process of the Main Staff and he was involved and active in it. Is there really any doubt that he knew what the plan was? Here's what he says on the 13th of July, this is General Tolimir. We know that he's assigned to oversee the situation in Zepa as one of the Main Staff generals, and he reported the ultimatum that he delivered to the Zepa Muslims. He said: "We made a condition that all necessary consultations be completed by 1500 hours and that the 'evacuation' had to start at that time. We have conditioned this with alternative solution -- with an alternative solution - military force." Hamdija Torlak, who you've heard from, recalled it this way. He says at transcript line 4292 -- or rather page 4292: "General Tolimir told us something along these lines: Srebrenica has fallen and now it's Zepa's turn. We can go about it two ways. What I'm offering is for all of you," meaning the entire Muslim population, "to leave Zepa, to be 'evacuated,' get on the buses and leave." Then he said there was nothing else to talk about. There was no negotiation. There was no agreement. And even if there were, the Tribunal's case law is clear in that that would not constitute a defence because whether or not somebody is forcibly transferred is something that has to be evaluated on an individual basis. Some government representative can't go in there and agree for someone else to be transferred. And our law is clear on this issue. There was no legitimate evacuation of the population, either of Srebrenica and Zepa. There was no combat going on and there was no need for those people to be evacuated. In fact, the law is clear that you cannot create the condition of exigency and then turn around and rely on it as a basis to commit another act. You can't create the crisis and then claim the crisis is the excuse to remove the population. That's clear too. You've heard evidence about the so-called 17 July declaration concerning the removal of the Muslim population, the one that was signed, it was signed by Franken, it was signed by Mandzic, and it was signed by Jankovic, who you've heard of course is General Tolimir's subordinate. In that declaration it claims: "No incidents were provoked by any side during the evacuation and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the international law of war." You will recall the testimony of DutchBat officer Robert Franken who explained to you how this was pure "nonsense." He explained that he signed the declaration with the reservation as concerns the UN observation or escort of vehicles or people from the enclave. He said he signed it because Jankovic, General Tolimir's subordinate, represented to him or certainly gave him the impression that it was a condition in order to get the wounded or evacuate the wounded. You'll also recall the testimony of PW-71 with respect to this declaration. The evidence concerning the 24 July agreement on disarmament of the able-bodied population in Zepa was no different. You heard Hamdija Torlak who told you unequivocally: "As far as our choices went, well, we didn't have any." UNPROFOR commander General Smith assessed the situation like this: "Let me be quite clear," he said, "the situation that the people wished to be evacuated from resulted from the collapse of the defence of the enclave and the presence of the Bosnian Serb army amongst them. "It was reported to me that you," meaning General Tolimir, "amongst others were in Zepa, that you and others were armed, and that you were telling the population to leave." This is at transcript page 11670. Edward Joseph testified in this case and he talked about speaking with the victims during the events and he was told, this is at Exhibit P1949, transcript line 14184, he was told this -- he asked whether somebody was leaving why the people were leaving, and he was told: "No, I'm not leaving of my own free will. I want to stay but who will protect me?" Someone else told him: "There is very ample" -- or rather, he testified that: "It was very ample and evident to us that these women were going out and leaving their homes under duress." General Tolimir was a key participant in the forcible transfer JCE and the evidence overwhelmingly proves that his contributions were not just at least significant, but they were substantial. Tolimir contributed personally and through the use of his sector and personnel to the VRS' relentless and ruthless implementation of directive 7's plan to bring the enclaves to their knees, to make life intolerable for the Muslim inhabitants, and ultimately to drive them out. The VRS engaged in terror attacks against Srebrenica in which Tolimir's sector played a vital part. I mentioned earlier the 23 June 1995 attack on the enclave. Tolimir's subordinates planned that operation. As my colleague mentioned, Colonel Salapura was involved in that planning, Vujadin Popovic was involved in that planning, Pavle Golic an intelligence officer with the Drina Corps, he was involved in that planning too, together with 10th Sabotage Detachment Commander Milorad Pelemis. Colonel Salapura testified that he didn't believe that General Tolimir was around at the time because had he been, he said, General Mladic's order to engage the 10th Sabotage Unit in the operation would have been passed from General Mladic via General Tolimir to Colonel Salapura. Unfortunately, that testimony was not as helpful to General Tolimir as Colonel Salapura probably hoped, because as it turns out General Tolimir was around on 23 June 1995. President Karadzic's appointment diary puts him at a meeting with Mladic, Petar Skrbic, who of course you've heard from, and Karadzic at Pale some 40 kilometres from Crna Rijeka at 1345 to 1500 hours on 23 July. You'll find that at P2198, the ERN reference there would be the ERN ending 5399. He's also caught in an intercepted communication together with General Mladic. That intercept, contrary to the Defence's challenge to the reliability, the accuracy, and the authenticity of the intercept collection, is on tape and you've got it. It's P779. Indeed, it would have been General Tolimir to approve of Colonel Salapura's proposal to use the 10th Sabotage Unit in that attack and it would have been General Tolimir who passed on General Mladic's approval or the order implementing the engagement of that unit. General Tolimir was a major player in the VRS' restriction of humanitarian aid convoys and also the military convoys. You will no doubt recall seeing his signature and initials all over convoy requests and related documents. General Mladic consulted with General Tolimir and General Gvero on these important issues. You will recall the testimony of numerous Prosecution witnesses who described the humanitarian conditions inside Srebrenica and Zepa, the effect of the restrictions of these convoys, from survivors to internationals. I won't go into that. These are all set out in the Prosecution's brief. You will remember the testimony of Slavko Kralj, the VRS Main Staff colonel, who initially sought to minimise General Tolimir's role in dealing with convoy issues. He had to concede when confronted with his prior testimony that indeed General Tolimir indeed had the authority to approve convoys second to General Milovanovic. Colonel Kralj testified that General Tolimir was "best versed" of all the Main Staff generals in respect of the procedures to be implemented regarding convoys. And as much as he tried to tone down General Tolimir's involvement in this process, in the decision-making process, tell-tale elements of his principal involvement in this emerged and they underscore the significance of his contributions. The Main Staff civil affairs department with respect to convoys acted on information it received from the "intelligence services" to deal with convoy requests. You may recall this, and I don't expect you to, but you may recall that I confronted Colonel Kralj about that reference to intelligence services. What did you mean by that? And he went round and round in circles trying to explain a way that that had anything to do with General Tolimir. Fundamentally, how could it not? General Tolimir, after all, was the top intelligence and security officer in the VRS. Anything to do with intelligence fell within his jurisdiction. Anything to do with security fell within his jurisdiction. That information that was relied on by the civil affairs department of the VRS was also furnished on a regular basis monitoring the aid that was going into the enclaves. So the Main Staff decision-making apparatus knew precisely what was going in and what wasn't going in. They knew precisely the extent to which they were cutting off the life-line of the Muslim populations inside those enclaves, and that's the civilian population. They knew this and they were monitoring. If you take a look at D209 you'll see exactly what I'm talking about and you'll see in that document that there's evidence that they had information about how much flour and oil and salt were going into the enclaves. They had precise details about what was going in, so they knew exactly what they were doing. The result of these restrictions on DutchBat you've heard, and you've heard lots of evidence about what effect that had and how it rendered them utterly incapable of carrying out their mandate to defend the enclaves. Tolimir was a part of all of that. General Tolimir also played a significant role in the lead-up to the attack on Srebrenica. You'll recall how he persistently misled and stalled and outright lied to UNPROFOR commanders about VRS intentions going in. In a July 9 communication, General Tolimir tells General Krstic: "I replied to the UNPROFOR commander that I was checking the information about the situation in Srebrenica and that their forces were safe. I anticipate talking to them in 40 minutes. Send a battle-field situation report every hour so that I can communicate with UNPROFOR which will enable you to continue to work according to plan." You'll recall the evidence of General Nicolai and others who dealt with General Tolimir as this plan was being executed. Remember that it was General Tolimir who passed on the 9 July approval of President Karadzic for the VRS to go into Srebrenica and take the town, which precipitated its fall on 11 July 1995 and the further displacement of thousands of Muslims. I would also like to remind the Chamber that throughout the meetings of the Hotel Fontana and the expulsion of the Muslim population from Potocari on 12 and 13 July, Tolimir's subordinates were on the ground and they were engaged. His immediate subordinates were there, his professional subordinates were there, and they were actively involved in the forcible transfer of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Radoslav Jankovic was there, Vujadin Popovic was there, Momir Nikolic was there, Svetozar Kosoric were there, in addition the Drina Corps MPs were involved as were Bratunac Brigade MPs. He directed them and he controlled them as he always did. Remember Tolimir was "exclusively responsible" for the correctness and legality for their work and that is the work of subordinate security organs, P1112. Of course he had to be and he was well informed of what they were doing. From 13 July on, Tolimir oversaw the removal of the Zepa population. As I mentioned earlier, he delivered the ultimatum to the Zepa Muslims, the threat of force, which the VRS of course backed up upon the Muslims' refusal to capitulate. He was directly involved in VRS efforts to neutralise UNPROFOR, to facilitate the take-down of the enclave, and the Chamber will recall the 14 July report to the Main Staff and General Krstic in which General Tolimir reports on the VRS having taken full control of check-point 2 at Boksanica, and he says: "We plan to direct the work of other UN check-points through this check-point." He says: "All check-points have received the task to remain at their current locations even after the VRS units have passed and to report to us on the activities of the Muslims." In charge of the operation to remove the Zepa population, Tolimir personally directed the operation until the last of them, that is, the population, Muslim population, had been expelled. He even personally removed men from a convoy who were then transferred to Rogatica prison and personally escorted the last convoy of the day on 25th July. Tolimir's contribution to the forcible transfer operation is clear, it is palpable, and it was substantial. The intensity of that contribution is matched to no lesser extent by his intent to use any and all force necessary to achieve its objectives. And Mr. McCloskey referred the Chamber to the 21 July proposal, the one proposing the use of chemical means. And what that document shows, Your Honours, is that General Tolimir was prepared to use whatever force and whatever means necessary to achieve the objectives to which he had been assigned to carry out, and that is the removal of the Muslim population from Zepa. There is no doubt that the intent of that document was to use that force against the civilian populations, which has been attested to by Colonel Obradovic and by General Savcic. At paragraph 358 of General Tolimir's brief he says, and I quote: "His role cannot be viewed in the context of events which took place at two not very large locations." And he's right. His role has to be viewed in terms of who he was to and in the Main Staff. It has to be viewed in terms of his involvement in Srebrenica and Zepa at the strategic level, the level of conception, of planning, of organisation, and of execution. It has to be viewed in the context of his favoured and influential position as a trusted member of General Mladic's inner core, and it has to be viewed in the context of his recognition and respect among the political leadership of the Republika Srpska. Viewed in this context, there's no doubt that he knew as well as anyone what the long-term goals were. He knew as well as anyone what the policies were. And he knew as well as anyone how the RS leadership and the VRS intended to reach those goals. He had to know in order to do his job and he had to know to be able to counsel and ably advise General Mladic, and he had to know in order to ensure the security of VRS operations. But the evidence in this case is much more than about what he knew. It's also about what he did and what he failed to do and what he intended. The evidence in this case proves all of this. Tolimir was as invested as General Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, Vujadin Popovic, Ljubisa Beara, Krstic, and others in achieving the Bosnian Serb war goals through manifestly criminal means. Tolimir was a key to the decision-making process of the VRS Main Staff. He personally participated and contributed to the forcible transfer. He oversaw and controlled his sector's involvement and the involvement of his subordinates both immediate and professional in the operation and in planning and implementing the conditions that brought misery and suffering to thousands of Bosnian Muslims. Your Honours, General Tolimir needs to be held to account for what he's done. Thank you for your indulgence. That concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. There are 15 minutes left. I see that Mr. Elderkin has already entered the courtroom. Would it be a wise proposal to have the second break now and that you, Mr. Elderkin, resume the last part of the session today with your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I think that would be preferable. I have around half an hour, as does Ms. Hasan, and I think my presentation would be cut in half if we took the break at the usual time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn now for the second break and I think you and Ms. Hasan should be aware of the wish of Mr. McCloskey to have ten minutes left at the end of today's hearing. We adjourn and we resume I would say ten minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin, welcome to the courtroom. You have the floor for your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. In this section of the closing arguments, I'm going to address opportunistic killings and the foreseeable targeted killings charged at paragraphs 22 and 23.1 of the indictment. My main focus today is to address Tolimir's liability for these killings because they were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove and deport the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa, in other words, a so-called JCE 3 crimes. However, Tolimir is also charged with all forms of Article 7(1) responsibility for these crimes under Counts 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of the indictment. As explained in detail in the Prosecution's final brief and as I'll reiterate today, the evidence of Tolimir's and his security and intelligence subordinates' involvement in the capture, detention, and disappearance of the Zepa leaders, and of Avdo Palic in particular, is compelling and he should be found guilty for those killings. He should be found guilty not just as the killings were the foreseeable consequences of the forcible removal JCE but because Tolimir authorised and approved the commission of those crimes as well as failed to protect these men who he and his subordinates had taken into custody. Looking first at the Srebrenica-related opportunistic killings, there is no need for me to repeat all of the evidence establishing that the killings took place; that's set out in the Prosecution's final brief. However, I will make a few remarks on some of those incidents. First, indictment paragraph 22.1(a) concerns the killing of nine Bosnian Muslim men who were found by DutchBat soldiers in a field some distance behind the white house in Potocari. This is discussed at paragraph 381 of the Prosecution brief. The Dutch eye-witnesses identified those victims who were found lined up by a stream with gun-shot wounds in their backs as Bosnian Muslims. In 2006 and 2007, human remains were exhumed from the meadow where the bodies were seen and these remains have been identified as Bosnian Muslim men reported missing mostly either from Potocari or from nearby. This evidence can be found in Exhibit P167 at pages 348 to 351 in e-court; also, the victims can be cross-referenced to the list of persons reported missing and dead after the take-over of the Srebrenica enclave, and that's Exhibit P1777. Second, indictment subparagraph 22.2 charges opportunistic killings in and around Bratunac when captured Srebrenica Muslims were taken there for temporary detention prior to the move up to the Zvornik area. The evidence of these killings is described at paragraphs 383 to 396 of the Prosecution brief. Notably there is support from at least one Bosnian Serb witness, PW-64, as well as Muslim survivors about killings in Bratunac. Those killings were taking place, of course, during the period when Tolimir's deputy or chief of security of the Main Staff Colonel Beara was in Bratunac busily making arrangements for those Muslim men to be transported north to the sites of mass execution. For the other opportunistic killing incidents charged, the relevant evidence is set out in the same part of the Prosecution's final brief, other than the killings at Petkovci school which are described at paragraphs 650, 651, and 656 of the brief. The opportunistic killings all took place in the days following the VRS's take-over of the Srebrenica enclave. The reason why they are charged as JCE foreseeable crimes, unlike the thousand of other killings of Bosnian Muslim males that took place after the attack on Srebrenica, is that they were not highly organised in the same way as the massive and complex operation which was supervised in particular by Beara and other of Tolimir's security and intelligence officer subordinates. Rather, they are killings like the one that happened in the centre of Srebrenica town where Your Honours may remember on the trial video seeing a man's body in a pool of blood, corresponding to Drazen Erdemovic's testimony that he saw one of his 10th Sabotage Detachment colleagues slit a man's throat near the central mosque. We can see this now on screen, that's from Exhibit P2799 at e-court page 43. If the opportunistic killings weren't organised and managed in the same careful way as the other massive scale killings in the murder operation, you may ask how Tolimir can be found liable for them. Indeed, this kind of question is raised in Tolimir's own final trial brief, where he dismisses JCE 3 as "just convict everybody." Of course JCE as a form of responsibility does not equate to "just convict everybody," but it is worth reminding Your Honours what it does take to convict a JCE member of crimes which go beyond the common shared goals. Simply put, what is required to find a JCE member guilty of a crime beyond the scope of the JCE is to find that the member chose to take part in serious criminal activity knowing that fellow members might commit additional crimes in the execution of the shared criminal enterprise. If Tolimir willingly took that risk, as he surely did, as evidenced most simply by the fact of his continued participation in the forcible removal JCE, then he should be convicted of such additional crimes as occurred. JCE 3 crimes must be the natural and foreseeable consequences of carrying out the JCE. The Appeals Chamber has ruled that foreseeable here means that: "The possibility a crime could be committed is sufficiently substantial as to be foreseeable to an accused." That's from a 25th of June 2009 decision in the Karadzic case. So the threshold is whether an accused could foresee that additional crimes not were probable but at least were possible. Applying this analysis to the charged opportunistic killings, what the evidence in this case shows is that Tolimir and indeed anyone else who would have been in such a high level, highly informed position within the VRS and with an interest in the consequences of operations such as the attack and ethnic cleansing of Srebrenica could foresee the possibility of fatal violence occurring. As heard throughout the trial, retaliatory violence between the warring parties had occurred in and around Srebrenica since 1992; furthermore, violence towards the Srebrenica Muslims was clearly foreseeable as part of the policy to ethnically cleanse areas claimed as Bosnian Serb land, including the Drina River valley, and generally it was foreseeable in light of the brutal history of the war. There can be no suggestion that Tolimir lacked knowledge of the historical build-up, hatred, and policy of ethnic cleansing that existed prior to July 1995. More specifically, the evidence demonstrates that Tolimir knew that murderous violence went hand in hand with ethnic cleansing operations. I'm now going to turn from the Srebrenica opportunistic killings to the foreseeable targeted killings of three of Zepa's religious, political, and military leaders, Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, and Avdo Palic. These men were taken into VRS custody while Tolimir oversaw the final stages of the removal of Zepa's civilian population in July of 1995. To emphasize how closely Tolimir was engaged with the fate of these men in the course of the forcible removal operation, UNPROFOR officer Tom Dibb saw Tolimir having Mehmed Hajric seized as the last buses were leaving from Boksanica on the 27th of July. Meanwhile, Avdo Palic had accompanied Tolimir as he led convoys of Muslims away from their homes to the confrontation line at Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, like your predecessors, you should slow down a bit. It's very difficult for the court reporter and the interpreters. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Palic was seen with Tolimir in the centre of Zepa on the 25th of July 1995. We can see another image taken from the stills book Exhibit P2799 at e-court page 163, showing Tolimir shaking hands with Palic in Zepa town on that day. And in fact that is the last known image that we have of Palic still alive, shaking hands with a man who clearly had power over his life or death. In terms of responsibility for Palic's fate in particular, it would not be much of an exaggerates to say that Tolimir practically chained Palic up himself. Shortly after Palic was taken into custody, Tolimir was sending out intelligence reports based on information he had obtained from Palic. Thereafter, Palic, whom the VRS considered to be a war criminal based on his involvement at the beginning of the war in an attack on a JNA convoy going up to Zlovrh mountain, Palic never had the hope of fair, humane, or legal treatment or any hope to see his wife and daughters again. Avdo Palic's last moments together with his family were movingly recounted to the Trial Chamber when Esma Palic herself came to testify. Avdo Palic was subsequently imprisoned at Rogatica Brigade security officer Zoran Carkic's apartment. Carkic then consulted with Beara in mid-August and Palic was moved at night to the secret Vaneko Mlin military prison in Bijeljina before being moved, again at night, in secret, in early September 1995, by Main Staff intelligence officer Dragomir Pecanac to a destination unknown. You'll recall Pecanac's account of taking Palic to hand him over in a car park in Han Pijesak in the middle of the night to an air force general, Jovo Maric, who, to fit well with Pecanac's story, died shortly after the war. But only after the East Bosnia Corps guards at that secret prison called the VRS Main Staff duty officer and received confirmation that Pecanac was acting on behalf of the Main Staff's sector for intelligence and security would they hand Palic over to Pecanac. Throughout those weeks of detention by the VRS security administration, Palic was not even referred to by name but by the code-name Atlantida, which we first saw in the 30th of July, 1995, document sent by Carkic on Tolimir's authorisation. That detailed how Atlantida was being kept safe and at a location away from the other Zepa Muslim detainees. That's Exhibit P1434. All of this evidence underscores the bare minimum conclusion that Tolimir could foresee the possibility that Palic might be killed. Tolimir knew of Palic's incarceration at the hands of men under his command and authority who only days before had been running the greatest murder operation in Europe since the Second World War. Given that Tolimir commanded and supervised those men who captured, detained, and then made Palic disappear, it seems almost trite to say it, but there can be no doubt that Tolimir foresaw that Palic might not or would not stay alive. Given the evidence, however, the Trial Chamber should not only convict Tolimir for the Zepa leaders' killings based on his JCE 3 liability, but also based on his acts and omissions recounted here and in the Prosecution final brief under the other charged forms of Article 7(1) liability. Those other forms of liability aside, to further emphasize the degree to which Tolimir could foresee the possible harm that might befall not only Palic but also Hajric and Imamovic, I would ask you to remember the words of General Mladic when he is seen on the trial video boarding bus after bus carrying the Muslim population out of Zepa. Mladic is being filmed and his words are clearly more for the camera than for the poor Muslims being driven from their homes. But as we can see on screen now, Exhibit P2798, this is a still shot from the trial video, you may remember that to one group Mladic says: "No more forgiveness. Now I am giving you your life as a gift." The VRS Main Staff leadership, particularly General Mladic of course, and also General Tolimir, was in charge of all decisions concerning the fate of the Zepa population, including having the power of life and death over the Muslims who passed through their hands. Tolimir, based on his background dealing with prisoner issues throughout the war, being informed about all key military events, and in the instance of the Zepa operation being actually involved and in charge on the ground, knew that particular Zepa Muslims including the leadership were at serious risk in the event that they were taken into military custody during the forcible removal operation. For Hajric, Imamovic, and Palic, they were not spared, not given their lives as a gift, but instead were captured, detained, and murdered before being dumped in the remote grave at Vragolovi, where their remains were recovered only after many years. I have referred in passing to the fact that Hajric, Imamovic, and Palic were not the only Zepa Muslims taken into custody by the VRS under Tolimir's and his subordinates' supervision. Over 40 other men, including Hamdija Torlak, another member of the Zepa leadership, were taken into custody and held in Rogatica at the same location as Hajric and Imamovic. All of those men were forced out of Zepa with the rest of the population in July 1995 but they only left VRS custody in a post-Dayton prisoner hand-over in January 1996. During the period while Hajric, Imamovic, and Palic were in custody and then disappeared, not only were other victims of the Zepa forcible removal operation being held in Rogatica, but the VRS was making great efforts to bring back the Zepa Muslims who had fled across the Drina River to Serbia. In addition, there was ongoing work to destroy public buildings and private homes in Zepa to deny the Muslims any possibility of return there. This is all also detailed in the Prosecution's final brief. What this shows is that the VRS's efforts to conclude the ethnic cleansing of Zepa continued after the last buses left Zepa town at the end of July 1995 and those efforts were ongoing at the time when the three leaders were detained and when they later disappeared. Accordingly, their murders undoubtedly occurred as the forcible removal JCE members sought to complete their work in cleansing Zepa of its Muslim population. Now I'd like to address some points that Tolimir has made concerning the Zepa killings in his final trial brief. At paragraph 478 Tolimir writes, I quote: "The basic questions regarding these alleged killings are the following: Who carried out these killings and under what circumstances and could Tolimir have reasonably foreseen them? Tolimir is not charged with participating in these killings." In response to the first point, it is not necessary to establish the particular identities of the killers, provided there is evidence beyond reasonable doubt that the Zepa Muslim leaders were murdered, which is shown by the circumstances of their disappearance and the result of the exhumation at the Vragolovi grave-site. The relevant forensic evidence is cited at paragraph 475 of the Prosecution's final brief. As for the circumstances of their disappearance, this is covered at paragraph 478. In response to the second point that "Tolimir is not charged with participating in these killings," as I said when I began, Tolimir absolutely is charged with all forms of Article 7(1) responsibility for these crimes, not just within the JCE framework. Again, I would remind Your Honours, as you have heard from Mr. Vanderpuye, that Tolimir had a duty to protect detainees and this applied to the Zepa leaders as much as to the men and boys captured after the fall of Srebrenica. Tolimir not only failed in this duty, but his actions through his subordinates, including Beara, Pecanac, and Carkic directly contributed to the deaths of Hajric, Imamovic, and Palic. Turning back to Tolimir's final brief, he goes on to give an account of the custody of Hajric, Imamovic, and Palic and at paragraphs 482 to 486 he describes the supposedly correct treatment of these prisoners before concluding as follows, I quote: "Considering that Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic were accommodated in an adequate holding centre, treated as prisoners of war, registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and allowed to send letters to their families, their alleged murder cannot be considered reasonably foreseeable. Tolimir's instructions contained in this document," Exhibit P1434, "provide additional confirmation that Tolimir took an interest in the correct treatment of the prisoners of war from Zepa." Furthermore, at paragraph 495 of his brief Tolimir notes, starting of quote: "Tolimir had already left for the for the Grahovo and Glamoc front on the 30 July 1995." As I emphasized when talking about the opportunistic killings, the question of foreseeability is indeed central to the analysis of Tolimir's liability for these killings pursuant to JCE 3. Therefore, it is important to look at the point Tolimir has made here, which is essentially that the conditions in which Hajric and Imamovic were held, the fact that they were registered with the Red Cross and that they were able to send messages to their families meant that the possibility they might be killed was not foreseeable to Tolimir, who departed to another part of the country at the end of July. In fact, the evidence received by the Trial Chamber points to the opposite conclusion, that Tolimir knew of the possibility that prisoners who appeared to be treated correctly were in fact at risk and his departure to Grahovo and Glamoc did not entail that he no longer knew what was going on in Eastern Bosnia. I've already discussed the extent to which Avdo Palic's killing was foreseeable to Tolimir. For Hajric and Imamovic, in general the foreseeability of their killings is covered in the Prosecution final brief. Specifically with regard to Tolimir's comments about Hajric and Imamovic's killings not being foreseeable because these victims were, to his knowledge, correctly treated and registered with the ICRC, that registration was a fig leaf to enable Tolimir and the VRS to claim that they treated prisoners in accordance with their duties under international law. The reality, as heard in the evidence, for example, of Meho Dzebo and Hamdija Torlak, is that the conditions at the Rogatica prison were appalling. Not only were conditions appalling, but the evidence clearly shows that Tolimir's security and intelligence subordinates, including VRS Drina Corps security chief Vujadin Popovic, those subordinates operated a system to facilitate the mistreatment and murder of prisoners in pure contempt of the ICRC's efforts to register them. I refer Your Honours to Popovic's 20th of September, 1995, instructions to cover up incidents where prisoners held by the VRS were killed in custody, that's Exhibit P2257 and also discussed at paragraphs 481 to 484 of the Prosecution's final brief. Clearly in accordance with these instructions from Popovic, the ICRC visitors to the Rogatica prison were told at the end of October 1995 that three of the men they had registered at the prison in July had "escaped since the last ICRC visit." Two of those three supposed "escapees" were Hajric and Imamovic and that ICRC report is Exhibit P2253. As further evidence that the registration or record keeping of captives did not preclude the possibility that they might be killed, I would also remind Your Honours of the fate of the Milici patients. Records were kept of those men during their hospital treatment, but they were nevertheless handed over to Vujadin Popovic and subsequently murdered. Indeed, the hand-over of the Milici patients to Popovic took place only shortly after Tolimir spoke to him on the 22nd of July and told Popovic to, I quote, "do your job." The story of the Milici patients reinforces the only reasonable conclusion, which is that in the circumstances after the Srebrenica murder operation Tolimir could foresee the possibility that even Muslims who had been registered or documented, whether by the ICRC or anyone else might be killed. As for Tolimir's departure to Grahovo and Glamoc on the 30th of July, being on the western front did not stop Tolimir, the assistant commander for intelligence and security, from keeping fully informed about matters in the east of the country. Just one example is Tolimir's 3rd of September, 1995, communication to various VRS intelligence and security subordinates. That's Exhibit P2250 which deals in particular with prisoner-related matters, including the situation concerning prisoners in Eastern Bosnia. I would like to end my presentation by reminding Your Honours of what we know of the final fate of Hajric, Imamovic, and Palic. For Hajric and Imamovic they were held in a prison cell known to the other prisoners in Rogatica as the infamous room. Meho Dzebo testified that they called it the infamous room because, I quote: "Because 90 per cent of the time that someone spent there, there was torture, beatings. One could hear cries, screams, cries for help and so son." Survivors from the infamous room confirmed to Dzebo that Hajric and Imamovic as well as another man, Mujo Hodzic whose remains were also found in the Vragolovi grave were among those regularly beaten. Sometime in August 1995 Hajric and Imamovic were taken away in the night. Meanwhile, we know that Palic was held in secret and separately. He was also finally taken away in the night in early September 1995 by a man, Dragomir Pecanac, who worked for Tolimir and whom Your Honours have seen here in this courtroom. We don't have evidence about Palic's treatment during his detention, but we do have evidence from his grave, the same as for Hajric and Imamovic. All three men were shot. The conclusion for the autopsy of Avdo Palic's remains reads in part, I quote: "The death was violent and it was caused directly due to the head injury. The fractures of the temple bone from the side of the upper jaw, ribs 5, 6, and 7 from the right side and 2, 3, 4, 6, 9 from the left side were caused by projectiles discharged from fire-arms." That's Exhibit P186. Your Honours, these three unfortunate men did not meet easy deaths nor did those men killed opportunistically following the fall of Srebrenica. They should be done justice, just as justice must be done for the thousands of other victims of the crimes charged in this case. That finishes my part of the presentation, Your Honour, and I think Ms. Hasan is following on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Welcome to the courtroom, Ms. Hasan. You have the floor now, but please be aware that Mr. McCloskey wants to have some minutes left at the end of today's hearing. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening to you. Good evening, Your Honours, and to everyone else. It is difficult, Your Honours, to speak about the impact of what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa in 1995. It is difficult to speak about the impact of events that have disgraced humanity. But I will try. The expulsion of the population of Srebrenica and Zepa as well as the separation and murders of thousands of Srebrenica men and boys irreparably destroyed the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. What remains are charred fragments of the population struggling for their existence until today. The society that remains in the aftermath of the events of July 1995 inflicted on them by the murderous criminal enterprise is a society in despair, a society that at once clings on to the past and is horrified to face the future, a society that has lost its leadership and its identity. Over the course of this trial you have received and heard evidence about the men who had to endure the painful separation from their families and the uncertainty that followed from not knowing what would happen to their loved ones and what their captors had in store for them. Their uncertainty was transformed to fear as they were forced to abandon their identification documents and personal belongings in Potocari, Sandici, and at other detention sites. Their captors' choice to detain them in the most deplorable and dehumanising conditions, to deprive them of their rights as human beings, their captors' choice to mistreat them converted their fear to sheer terror. These men endured terrifying moments as they were taken on buses and trucks, in some instances blindfolded and handcuffed to preselected execution sites. Over 7.000 men and boys endured this incomprehensible horror and pain before they faced a violent and merciless death. Few men survived these horrendous slaughters and some of them have had the courage to sit here before you and to relate to you their ghastly experiences. It was not that long ago that a miracle, PW-21, was in our presence, a boy who against all odds emerged alive from the mass execution at Orahovac. He witnessed the unfathomable, the murders of hundreds of men surrounding him, including his own father. Other fortunate survivors have told you how they narrowly escaped their deaths. You may recall, for example, PW-18 who after being severely beaten and shot, after witnessing his relatives' executions, found the strength somewhere in him and played dead on the hills of Nezuk as blood spewed from his mouth. This was the state he was in when he escaped execution. Remember PW-15, he took cover under a mass of people who had been executed before his eyes in Petkovci. These men suffered physical injuries and immense mental anguish. All of them, those that were killed and those that escaped, endured profound horror at the hands of the joint criminal enterprise. After being uprooted from their homes, their land, their surroundings, and all that was familiar to them, the Bosnian Muslim women of Eastern Bosnia were made to endure the intense heartache as they were torn from their relatives in Potocari before being expelled to Kladanj. These final separations caused stress and anxiety amongst the women upon their arrival in Bosnian territory and continue to traumatise them some 16 years later. Your Honours, you have received the accounts of a number of Srebrenica widows and victim relatives, and I refer you to their statements, but I wish here now to give them a voice so that you hear a few of their words in this courtroom. The impact of the separations was described by Razija Pasagic, who said, and I quote: "The experience of being separated from my husband, my brother, and my friends was very difficult. I lived, but actually my life does not exist, or can we say my life goes on but I do not exist." The murders of the men was a monumental step towards the destruction of the women and children. For years the Bosnian Muslim women of Eastern Bosnia have lived in perpetual uncertainty and turmoil wondering what happened to their loved ones, burdened and tormented by thoughts of how their loved ones died, where they died, whether they were tortured, whether they were hungry. You have heard compelling evidence about the Srebrenica syndrome and the psychological trauma experienced by these women. Teufika Ibrahimefendic from the Vive Zene organisation has described to you the symptoms these women have suffered from, amongst them terrible nightmares, feelings of fear, nervousness, and aggressiveness. Their will to live was extinguished. These women suffer from pronounced guilt, many wishing they would have died. Hanifa Hafizovic, and you have also received her statement which is Exhibit P1522, has said: "You can't go against God, but if God showed me mercy tomorrow and I died I would be happy." Other women engage in self-destructive behaviours. And in addition to their mental suffering, many of these women suffer physically. With the advent of DNA matching, the women and children began learning about the fate of the missing men after many, many years, but they were not freed from the shackles of their misery when they received this information, the confirmation that their loved ones were in fact dead, that only body parts remained, and that in many cases only few body parts were found, that these body parts were spewed in mass graves at locations unknown to them. The reburial operation denied these women of a decent burial in accordance with their religious and ethnic customs. This also aggravating their mental suffering. It is difficult, Your Honours, to speak of any long-term recovery for these women, even for those we have heard who have received treatment. Their condition is still extremely grave and today the condition of some of them has even worsened. The Srebrenica syndrome still plagues many women and families, as not all reported missing men have been identified. Innumerable women and families still live without knowing. Some perhaps will never know. Recall Mirsada Malagic, her father-in-law, Omer Malagic, was only buried some three years ago. Her husband and her middle son were recently buried in 2010. We know that the mortal remains of her son Admir Malagic were located in the secondary mass grave you are now familiar with, Cancari road 6, primarily associated with the Branjevo farm executions. The remains of her husband Salko Malagic were found at Cancari road 10, also associated with the Branjevo farm executions. Her father-in-law was recovered from the secondary mass grave at Cancari road 3, associated with the Kozluk executions. Her eldest son, Elvir Malagic, who was 19 years old in July of 1995, remains missing. Elvir would have been 36 today. Time has stopped for Mirsada Malagic. She still waits, like thousands of others suffering, uncertain about the fate of her son. Many women have hoped against hope, like Samila Salcinovic whose evidence you have also received. She doesn't want to remarry because she hopes that her husband will appear. Her statement can be found at Exhibit P1524. The story of Mirsada Malagic, Samila Salcinovic, and all the other Srebrenica widows the Prosecution has presented to you are just a handful of the thousands of tragic stories of other families of the enclaves of Eastern Bosnia, families that have been dismembered and dispossessed. We have heard evidence that cohesive family units no longer exist. We have heard how those who once led social lives now isolate themselves and have developed fear and distrust of groups. We have learned that these survivors do not find any solace in numbers. Nura Efendic, a Srebrenica widow who not only lost her husband but also her two sons, said that the fact that she was not the -- tells herself that she's not the only one in this situation. Knowing that, she says, "there are thousands of us" is of no consolation to her. General Tolimir, a core member of the VRS, of the highest echelon of the VRS, and who lived and worked in the region, was intimately aware of the importance of the men in the traditional patriarchal societal structure of the Bosnian Muslims in Eastern Bosnia. By killing two or three generations of these men from Srebrenica, the Bosnian Serb forces and Tolimir knew and intended the catastrophic consequences the killings would have on the entire group. Eliminating the pillars of that society, the men and the leaders, guaranteed the collapse of the surviving members. As a result, certain family names are disappearing. The family name of Hanifa Hafizovic, for example, will disappear as 18 male members of her family went missing after the fall of Srebrenica. There are no men left to carry that family name forward. The grief and trauma of these women resulting from the killing of the men was compounded by their expulsion. They have not been able to re-establish their lives. The evidence shows that a lot of these families led reasonably prosperous lives before the war under the guidance and protection and leadership of their husbands and fathers. Witness Rahima Malkic, as she put it, had "a nice life." She lived with her children and husband, worked their land, they owned sheep, cows, a horse, had chickens. They owned one house and were even constructing another house. But after having been uprooted from their homes in July of 1995 and having lost the male members of their family, life changed. And now they struggle to make ends meet. The vast majority of these women have not been able to reclaim their lives to find employment to support their families, and have been forced to live in makeshift accommodation for many years. Samila Salcinovic, a newlywed at the time of the fall of Srebrenica, lost nine male members of her family, including her husband. She found herself a refugee. She could not find a job and grows vegetables on a small piece of land, lives with no running water, and relies -- in her home, and relies on a well for water, but that well drys up in the summer. The Bosnian Muslim women of Eastern Bosnia have suffered profoundly from the difficulties they have faced from taking on the responsibilities that used to be fulfilled by the men in that society. These men -- these women used to rely on their men who were more educated to take care of official family business and to financially support them. The members of the criminal enterprise were fully cognizant that by killing the men they were going to profoundly disrupt the foundations of this group as a whole. The physical destruction of the homes and the sacred places in Srebrenica and Zepa described in the Prosecution's brief at paragraphs 470 to 473 in relation to Zepa at paragraph 377 -- sorry, that's paragraph 377 is in relation to Srebrenica, as well as the killing of the men and the physical and mental suffering resulting from the killing of the men and the expulsion of the women has prevented those who survived from returning home. You may recall Mirsada Malagic's response when she was asked why she would not go back to her home. She said: "It's impossible to live there." She explained, and I quote: "Anyone who survives Srebrenica, who survived the war, who went through everything that I went through, believe me, cannot live there." Rahima Malkic, who you did not hear testify but whose evidence was admitted, asked: "How can I go back there when half my family is not there?" Her husband and two sons went missing after the fall of Srebrenica, and so she asks: "How can I rebuild my house? I don't have any men who could help me." The women feel they cannot return to their homes alone and in most cases they don't have any homes to return to. Nothing remained in Zepa. Their homes were burnt down. There are no factories or jobs left to return to. Many of Zepa's inhabitants have resettled in other parts of the world, as the conditions in Zepa as testified by Esma Palic were "not fit for life." Nor do the Bosnian Muslim youth of Eastern Bosnia want to return. They dream of leaving Bosnia all together. And let us not forget those Bosnian Muslim youth of Eastern Bosnia, those that survived face significant hurdles suffering from adjustment problems such as low levels of concentration, nightmares, flashbacks, fears, and behavioural problems. Those who have lost their fathers, their uncles, their grandfathers, lack male role models which has affected their transition to adulthood, their families, and their sense of identity. What is sure is that the impact of this murderous operation will be significant for them for years to come. The impact of the ethnic cleansing on the population of Srebrenica and Zepa as well as the separation and cold murders of the men has caused incalculable suffering and damage to the tens of thousands of living survivors who have been condemned to a lifetime of physical and mental suffering. The impact on the group as a whole has been catastrophic. And this end result was purposeful. It was intended that there be no hope for further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa. I have tried, Your Honours, to capture the pervasive and stifling impact on the individuals and the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia as a whole, but it is perhaps best to leave you with the words of Amer Malagic, a relative of Srebrenica victims, who has said: "Imagine what this has done to our families, and it is worse." This, Your Honours, is the impact of the death of more than 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men of Eastern Bosnia and the expulsion of the remaining population, this is the indescribable pain of thousands of families. This, Your Honours, is the intended deep and lasting impact of the culpable decisions and actions of the RS leadership, of the VRS, and of General Tolimir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Hasan. Now, Mr. McCloskey, you get the floor again exactly for ten minutes, as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have much to say further. Words that I had on my paper and meant to say somehow after my friends and colleagues' presentations don't have the worth I thought they may have been. So I want to remind you of one thing and that is: General Tolimir, when we look at his intent, did he make this horrible crime his own or was he just someone that assisted along the way? We know that General Tolimir is a very bright, very impressive, one of the top three, four people of this hideous Main Staff and their ethnic cleansing. He stands as an example of VRS soldierdom, of -- and his actions are something that will be looked upon and judged in history. He is a man that acts with his own free will. He voluntarily chose the path he took. When he was delivered this murder operation by General Mladic and his orders, he had several choices. He wilfully, voluntarily, and intentionally chose loyalty to Mladic, loyalty to the cause over his duty as a soldier and a man to stand down, his duty to his God to say no, his duty under law to stop and prevent and protect. He never uttered a word to the ICRC, to the press, to anyone to stop this or do anything about it. He adopted it for his own for the purposes of the VRS, for the purposes of Mladic. We have never heard him utter a negative word against his leader and his loyal commander General Mladic. He, in choosing Mladic over law, has lost his humanity, but he did this on his own under his own free will. He is not someone that is merely assisting in this project or aiding and abetting. He represents this awful expulsion and destruction. This unique Srebrenica genocide is something that he carries with him personally and will forever. There is only one sentence for this crime and that is life imprisonment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. I take it that this concludes the final oral submission of the Prosecution. We're now nearly at the end -- we are now at the end of today's hearing. Tomorrow Mr. Tolimir will present his views during his final oral submissions. There's nothing that we have to deal with today, therefore we adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15, in this courtroom, number 3. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
